Labour Conditions-Wages Control

subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE

speechtext: Right Hon. AV. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister): I should like to say a word with respect to the war-time wages control order.

subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext: The Prime Minister just got in ahead of me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend will not hold that against me.
May I read to the house a paragraph which appears in the speech from the throne at the closing of the last session. The paragraph is as follows; Hansard, page 5575:
During the course of the year, the price ceiling has been splendidly maintained. My ministers have reaffirmed their determination to do all in their power to prevent inflation snd to safeguard a basic standard of living. To this end the war-time wages control order has been simplified and strengthened. It will continue to be administered by the national war labour board. Consultation is proceeding *with the several provinces regarding the enactment of a comprehensive code of labour relations which will be administered by a war-time labour relations board, and "which will include the principle of compulsory collective bargaining.
May I speak first on the second of these matters, the one related to a code of labour relations. I am happy to be able to say to the house that the consultations which were proceeding between the provinces and the dominion have been concluded, and there have also been concluded consultations between representatives of labour organizations and the government with respect to the code. I am advised that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), expects to 'be in a position to table early next week the enactment respecting the code of labour relations.
As to the war-time wages control order, many representations have been made to the government, some by hon. members of the house, some from labour organizations and others from other sources. These the government has already had under consideration. To-morrow the government will be meeting a delegation of representatives of the Canadian Congress of Labour. As hon. members know, there are four outstanding labour organizations representative of the different labour unions throughout the country: the one which I have just mentioned, the Canadian Congress of Labour; another organization, also large in numbers, older in years, the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada; there is the Canadian Catholic Confederation of Labour; and there are the organizations representing the railway brotherhoods. On January 27 of this year the government met 100-21
the joint legislative committee of the railway running trade organizations as a delegation from that body. At that time certain representations were made to the government with respect to the war-time wages control order. Tojmorrow, as I have said, the government will be meeting the delegates of the Canadian Congress of Labour, and we expect that representations will be made by that body to the government with respect to this order. At any rate I now extend an invitation to the delegates of the Canadian Congress of Labour to make such representations as they feel they may wish to make to the government with respect to the order.
A^ery shortly the government will be meeting a delegation of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada and also a delegation from the Canadian Catholic Confederation of Labour. These are the customary annual meetings with the government. AAre will expect, and I now invite, the delegates of these other large organizations to make to the government such representations as they deem advisable with respect to the war-time wages control order.
AVhen the government has these various representations before it, the government will then be in a position further to consider what amendments should be made to the order. It is the intention of the government to make certain amendments, but we wish to have these representations from the leading labour organizations before us when we are considering these further amendments; and after that opportunity has been given to labour, and the government has had the opportunity of considering all representations which have been made, amendments will be made by the government to the war-time wages control order.
I would hope that these various labour organizations could meet with the government within the next two weeks. One meeting as I have said has been arranged for to-morrow. I do not know that there has been a definite date fixed for the other two; but I would say now that we would seek to meet their convenience at as early a date as may be possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister rose to make a statement with respect to the war-time wages control order of 1943, I rather expected that he would make a much more comprehensive and perhaps much more satisfactory statement than he did, and having that in mind, I suggested that he was "getting there first", before I had asked my question. But I want to say this to the Prime



Labour Conditions-Wages Control
Minister: as he rose, I was about to make an inquiry, and it was on this basis. What the Prime Minister has now said in connection with calling in the other representatives is, of course, a very good thing. I hope he will do that. I hope he will give some real consideration to what they say. But in the meantime February 15 is the deadline for the operation of the war-time wages control order of 1943, and that is where the emergency and urgency of the matter arise. May I ask the Prime Minister, as I intended to before this statement was made, that the government give consideration to the postponement of the application of war-time wages control order of 1943; otherwise it will go into effect and then all the representations that are afterwards made cannot be regarded in perhaps the same light as those which are made before the order goes into effect. At the same time, and following up what the Prime Minister has said, and doing what the Prime Minister now suggests be done in another way, I suggest that he refer this whole order to the industrial and international relations committee of the house, so that those interested in and affected by the provisions of the order may have an opportunity to appear before that committee.
These two suggestions, I think, are most important, and I impress them upon the Prime Minister: first of all, the postponement of the application of the wages control order-because it is going to be too late by the time he sees all these people-and second, that the parliamentary committee have a chance to hear the representations of these people in a proper way. I ask the Prime Minister to give consideration to these suggestions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext:
I am always pleased to give consideration to any suggestions which my hon. friend may wish to make.
He has referred to the 15th of this month being the date on which the order itself takes effect in some particulars. In that connection, there is one very important consideration, it is that there are certain benefits which accrue to labour, under the order, on the 15th. They relate to the basic wage in which the cost of living bonus is embedded; and I understand that already steps have been taken by employers to see that the benefits to be derived from that section in particular will be accorded. It would I think be inadvisable to postpone anything of the nature of a benefit. I cannot see that there would be any possibility of anything inimical happening from effect being given the order in other particulars as, in fact, is now the case, before the further representations of labour have been heard. I assure my hon. friend that the government is most anxious in this matter, (Mr. Graydon.]
above all others, to have the cooperation of labour. We believe that labour, as well as all other classes in the community, is interested in preventing inflation in this country, and that labour realizes that a measure of wage stabilization is essential if we are to preserve the price ceiling. We all recognize that it will require close and helpful cooperation on the part of government, labour, employers and the community, to maintain the price ceiling and prevent inflation. We have no desire to be in any way coercive in this matter, but rather we wish to make the measure as effective as it can be made through good will on the part of all parties concerned. At a later stage it might be advisable to have the committee which my hon. friend has mentioned, the committee on industrial and international relations, consider some of these matters. If so, I should be prepared to advise my hon. friend accordingly; but at the moment I think the step proposed by the government will expedite the revision of the order in a manner which will help to meet at least some of the objections, and I should hope all fundamental objections.

subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext: If I may ask one supplementary question, the Prime Minister mentioned that the national labour code would be brought into being by order in council, as the war-time wages control order was brought into being. May I ask the right hon. gentleman if, in view of the dissatisfaction that has been expressed at the way this order was put through, by order in council, the government will not bring in legislation dealing with the national labour code, so that this house may properly consider all the aspects relating to labour relations in Canada, instead of doing it by order in council as was done in connection with the wages control order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext:
The government has carefully considered the matter to which my hon. friend has just referred. One thing we must keep before us at the present time is the fact that these are temporary measures. We are not enacting permanent legislation. These measures are being enacted for the purpose of meeting conditions relating to the war. How long the war will last none of us can say, but it is certain that as conditions in the world change some of these orders will have to be changed considerably. To bring into parliament legislation which would be as comprehensive as these measures are; to have that legislation considered by this house, in addition to the heavy legislative programme already before the house, I fear would not be helpful in enabling us to keep our minds con-

Air Force
centrated above all else on the prosecution of the war itself. There are important war measures that must be taken up ahead of all other legislation, they have been mentioned to the house already. I submit that parliament itself enacted the War Measures Act to enable the government to meet by order in council situations arising out of the war, and this is the kind of ehactment it was intended should be dealt with under that act.

subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext: When parliament is in session? That is just rendering us impotent.	,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext: No. I think my hon. friend is overlooking the very important consideration I just mentioned, namely that parliament should be giving its attention to the most important war measures and not be devoting its time to discussing at considerable length measures that are solely in the nature of temporary measures, which can be dealt with effectively under the provisions of an act of parliament passed for the very purpose of meeting such conditions.

subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext:
That
means we are to abdicate our functions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext: I think I am expressing the position in a way that will be regarded as sensible and will be readily understood by all. I should add this further word. The enactment, presented in this form, is a flexible measure the provisions of which may be altered by order in council, just as the enactment itself is by order in council. That is very different from the procedure required to amend a statute. One could not say whether parliament would be in session at the moment at which a statute might have to be amended. On all counts, taking these various points into consideration, the government believes that the supremacy of parliament will be fully maintained by the power which is being exercised under its authority in this way. Certainly by this procedure the time of parliament will be preserved for the discussion of the most important of all measures.

subtopic: WAR-TIME WAGES CONTROL ORDER-LABOUR RELATIONS CODE
speechtext: In the light of the Prime Minister's statement as to the advantages to labour contained in order in council P.C. 9384, I should like to ask if any organized body of labour has suggested that they would like to have this order applied on February 15 because of those advantages.

I cannot answer my hon. friend categorically, but I do know that some of the labour organizations feel that there will be substantial benefits to them under this order and would welcome those benefits coming into effect on the 15th of this month.

POLICY WITH RESPECT TO RETIREMENT OF OFFICERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a further question of the minister. In view of the recentfy reported retirement of a large number of high ranking officers of the Royal Canadian Air Force, has he any statement to make to the house in the matter?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: POLICY WITH RESPECT TO RETIREMENT OF OFFICERS
speechtext:
My hon. friend was good
enough to give me notice of the question. In reply I may say that there is a definite retirement policy in the Royal Canadian Air Force.
When the war broke out the R.C.A.F. was a small organization. It comprised a number of excellent officers who had done magnificent service in the last war. These men were the backbone of the R.C.A.F. development and expansion. The principal job of the R.C.A.F. during the first years of the wrar wras the organization, development, expansion and administration of the air training plan. The plan has produced results and dividends far surpassing our own expectations and frustrating those of our enemies.
These officers, who gave of their time and experience to bring about those results, though comparatively young in years, were mainly too old to take an active operational part in this war. Besides, their experience, their prestige, their authority, made it necessary to retain them here or elsewhere in non-operational duties.
fMr. Power.]
The rapid expansion of the joint air training plan, the western hemisphere operations and the overseas air force brought increased responsibilities and with these accelerated promotion. There are now many officers of comparatively high rank in our forces who have not seen operational service. They could not. But rapid promotion brings the penalty of early retirement, otherwise there would be stagnation at the top. The air war and the air force must be dynamic, not static.
The air training plan has reached its peak of development. From now on there will be contraction rather than expansion. The favourable war situation has brought about a shifting and contraction of our defensive home war establishments.
If all these men were retained in their positions or promoted right up to their full retiring age we might be faced -with a thick ceiling, a bottle-neck at the top, comprised entirely of men who, through no fault of their own, have seen no active flying service overseas in this war. Now, after five years of war, we have at our disposal, overseas especially some younger men who have had actual fighting experience against the enemy in this war. More and more we are calling on overseas headquarters to send these men back to us.
If we are to encourage the initiative, the ambition of these young men, we must show them that there is room at the top, that the ceiling is not closing in, but that the upward path will be made clear for them.
This is the policy. There is no stigma, no reproach in retirement, but there is ruthless necessity if the R.C.A.F. is to continue during the war and after to be the young, virile, dynamic force which I am sure all Canada wishes it to be and has a right to expect from it in return for the sacrifices made on its behalf.

I should have saidi that, first of all, they were asked as to whether they would wish to have such a meeting. All the provinces, I believe, have signified their readiness to meet with the dominion government in conference on matters of mutual interest and concern in connection with social security, health, and other matters-financial matters being among that number.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Labour I should like to reply to a question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas).
Conscientious objectors who have dependents are in camps as a result of a magistrate's
The Address-Mr. Marshall

decision due to refusal to comply with the regulations. Men of this class when declared to be conscientious objectors are given the opportunity of performing alternative service by assigning a part of their wages to the Canadian Red Cross and adjustments are made in the amount of the assignment so that the man will be able to maintain his dependents.
There are certain cases, however, where individuals will not accept any direction at all, and in these cases it has been necessary to have them committed to service camps. Unfortunately their dependents have to rely upon their own resources, these cases being parallel to the cases of men committed to a prison. These men are encouraged to reconsider their decision, and when this happens the arrangements originally proposed to them are put into effect.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, February 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. L. D. Tremblay for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Graydon, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Roy.
Mr. ,1. A. MARSHALL (Camrose): Mr. Speaker, if I were allowed only sixty seconds in which to express an opinion upon the proposals to be found in the throne speech, I would say two things. First, these proposals serve only to relieve and not to cure. They are merely palliatives. My second thought is that all reforms depend upon monetary reform.
Canada in the matter of production ranks high among the nations of the world. Human effort, combined with material resources and unfettered by financial limitations, has raised Canada to a position where she is admired, where she is the envy of the whole world. There flow from Canada's shores to-day vast quantities of war materials and foodstuffs, not only to our own fighting men and women but to every 'one of the allied nations. Such an achievement is highly creditable and reflects upon the wonderful work which is being done by our men and women in industry, in mining, in fishing, in forestry and on the farm. I should like too to pay a tribute to the men and women of our fighting forces, who are to be found not only in our own country but in Great Britain and in almost every theatre

of war. They are doing a magnificent job; they are writing history which future generations will read with pride and satisfaction.
I was deeply impressed by the speech made several days ago by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). Here is a man who has spent three years in close association with Canadian men and women in Africa, in Sicily, and in Italy. He has come to know their thoughts, their dreams, their aspirations, their plans, and their difficulties. He has returned to this country, and at the first opportunity has presented these difficulties to us as members of the House of Commons. I believe he deserves the support of every hon. member in his endeavour to get these wrongs righted. I for one shall be glad to give him every support in this work
But there is one thing I should like to say at this time. Just as long as Canada is fettered with an outworn financial system, just so long will it be difficult for us to bring about necessary reforms. As the editor of the Ottawa Citizen aptly expressed it the other day: Reform our monetary system and ninety per cent of the ills of society will be cured. There must be no financial restrictions to Canada's post-war programme, but I fear that as long as the go\'ernor of the Bank of Canada, the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board and the deputy minister of finance are the chief advisers to this or any other government, there is little hope of much change in our financial policy.
On February 11 of last year, within a day of one year ago, I spoke during the debate on the throne speech. On that occasion I said I believed that forces were at work which had as their object the accomplishment of three things: (1) the return of Canada to the gold standard; (2) the establishment of a supranational government, backed up by an international police force; and (3) the complete destruction of British idealism, individualism and initiative and the substitution therefor of state autocracy. Any rightthinking individual who has been following the course of events through the newspapers can readily see that these objectives will eventually be attained unless some action is taken to thwart the move.
I turn now to the speech from the throne itself. We find in it, as someone aptly expressed it to me the other day, a strange mixture of pious platitudes and ponderous piffle. In support of my first assertion I read

The Address-Mr. Marshall
the third paragraph of the speech from the throne:
The winning of the war clearly remains the first of all objectives. My ministers believe it is their duty to see that Canada's war effort is firmly maintained until the enemy is defeated in Europe and in Asia. They believe the government's primary task, and the primary duty of the Canadian people, is to concentrate on the prosecution of the war. Our fighting men must he assured that there will be no diversion from this vital task and no relaxation of Canada's war effort. Till the war is won, the policies of my government will continue to be shaped to that end.
Our armed forces at sea. on land and in the air have added lustre to the name of Canada.
Those are wonderful words, and I agree heartily with the sentiments there expressed. But in the mind of the common man in this country, confusion and doubt and anxiety exist with respect to the trend of events at the present time. It is difficult for the common man to understand when he picks up his newspaper and reads that General McNaughton has given up the command of the Canadian forces, the reason given being ill health, to find a few days later that that statement is contradicted and the government take no action to clear up the puzzle. It is difficult, too, for the common man to understand why it is that when Russia and the United States are fighting as allies, Russia is attacking Finland while the United States is still on friendly relations with that country. It is difficult, too, for the common man to understand why it is that when Britain and the United States are locked in deadly combat with Japan, Russia, which is our ally, gives to the Japanese valuable fishing concessions in Russian waters. It is little wonder that doubt and confusion and anxiety exist in the minds of the people of Canada. It is little wonder that our people do not understand what Lord Yansittart meant when he said just a short time ago, in an article appearing in an English periodical, that this is a phoney war and we may get a phoney peace.
Now I turn to the second assertion which I made. In the seventh paragraph of the speech from the throne I read this:
Canada's prosperity and the well-being of her people are bound up with the restoration and expansion of world trade. Export markets are essential to the efficient employment of vast numbers of Canadians. Larger _ imports are needed to raise the standard of living.
That is a strange statement. It leads me to believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is still living in the ox-cart age of economics. This whole question of foreign trade, export markets, imports, and so
forth, was I think very satisfactorily dealt with by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) when he spoke the other day, but because the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) showed the same deplorable lack of knowledge of economics yesterday, I think it is necessary for me to bring a little more evidence to bear on the matter.
I have here a copy of a report of the London Chamber of Commerce on "General Principles of a Post-War Economy". This was published on the 12th of May, 1942, and is the outcome of a study by a special committee appointed by the council of the London Chamber of Commerce on March 10, 1942. In order that hon. members may get a picture of the background of the London Chamber of Commerce, may I read the first paragraph of the report:
The London Chamber of Commerce has a direct membership of 9,000 firms and companies. Thirty-nine industrial and commercial associations, with an approximate membership of 50,000, are affiliated to it and are represented on its council. The chamber is therefore vitally concerned in the nature of the framework within which industry and commerce will be called upon to function after the war.
The special committee appointed by the council studied this whole question of markets, imports and exports, favourable and unfavourable balances, and tariffs. I quote from pages 8 and 9:
It is an obvious absurdity that nations should regard it as necessary to export their real wealth, not for the purpose of paying for imports, hut in order to solve their domestic unemployment problem by passing it on to other countries. Exports with this end in view are nothing more nor less . than an excuse for distributing wages to people who otherwise wmuld be unemployed. This purpose would be equally well served if the goods were to be thrown into the sea or if the people were to be employed to dig holes and to fill them up again.
When, however, it is remembered that even wealthy nations have a large percentage of their population under-fed, ill-clothed and ill-housed, it is clear that these would be the best recipients of this alleged surplus wealth. What is necessary is to improve the technique for the internal provision of money, so as to convert this human demand into effective demand.
The chamber considers that it is a perversion of export trade to employ it for the purpose of exporting domestic unemployment and dumping it on other nations which already have their own problem to solve. These surplus exports might confer a benefit on some countries if they were sent as a gift; and the recipient country had an interal financial mechanism capable of distributing enough purchasing power to its people to enable them to buy excess imports oi consumers' goods in addition to, instead of in competition with, the goods already there. They are. on the contrary, used for the purpose of getting other nations into unpayable debt; and moreover, the recipient nations have not the
32S
The Address-Mr. Marshall

mechanism for distributing additional purchasing power to buy them so that they do, in fact, displace goods already in the market, and cause distress selling and a slump in prices.
The chamber submits that international trade must now be raised to its true function, that is, nothing more nor less than an exchange of goods and services of a mutually advantageous character.
I would like hon. members to compare this with the unrealistic attitude of the government on this question as given in the speech from the throne. In the language of the air force the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture are off the beam and lost in fog.
The question in my mind which I have to answer to my own satisfaction as I study the proposals is simply this: To what extent will they solve present and future national problems? The amendment of the Progressive Conservative party and the amendment of the Bloc Populaire are of little concern to me; they are designed to put people on the spot. They are nothing more or less than political by-plays.
What are some of the things which we propose to do in this session of parliament? We are told that the government proposes to set up three departments-a department of veterans' affairs, a department of reconstruction and a department of social welfare. We are asked to approve of Canadian participation in the establishment of an international organization to further national security through international cooperation. We are asked to give approval to an industrial bank. We are asked also to approve of housing legislation, a nation-wide health insurance plan, contributory old age pensions, provision for family allowances, and a price floor for staple farm products. In a word, all this legislation means bureaucracy, regimentation, and cruel taxation, if carried out under the present economic set-up.
I believe that members of parliament, in discussion, are constantly confusing two things, methods and objectives. These proposals in the throne speech are methods whereby we can attain a certain objective. So far as I can learn, very few members have discussed paragraph 10, which deals with the objective this government has set for the Canadian people.
Let me say at the outset that objectives are not the concern of members of parliament or of cabinets; objectives must come from the people themselves, and if they do not come from the people themselves they are of little value. Paragraph 10 of the speech from the throne sets out the post-war objective:
While the post-war objective of our external policy is world security and general prosperity, the post-war objective of our domestic poliey is social security and human welfare.
[Mr. Marshall.1?
It is strange that we should place our foreign policy ahead of our domestic policy. We have given it precedence in the speech from the throne. The reason for this is not clear. It is not my intention at the moment to discuss the question of foreign policy, but I wish to say one or two words with reference to the post-war objective of our domestic policy. We are told that that objective is social security and human welfare. The inmates of a gaol or penitentiary or an asylum enjoy those things; they have social security and welfare. The slaves in the early days enjoyed the same condition. The people of Germany, the people of Italy and the people of Japan enjoyed a high standard of social security and human welfare, but two things they did not enjoy were individual freedom and personal initiative. It is strange that these things are not to be found in the domestic objectives as outlined in the speech from the throne. I say that the people will reject this objective when they come to realize what it all means. I think I am safe in saying that what the people of my constituency, one hundred per cent of them, want is economic security with individual freedom; and I cannot support that part of the throne speech unless the Prime Minister and his advisers are prepared to make those necessary changes.
In order to obtain these objectives, methods are suggested. To me, methods are clearly the responsibility of experts. Neither the mass of the people of Canada nor the members of parliament are experts, so that I do not think that we are in much of a position to judge the merits and demerits of these various proposals. My opinion is that it is the business of members of parliament to frame and place upon the statute books of Canada laws which will make these proposals effective. Therefore, we must first settle upon the objective. Having settled upon our objective, we should retain the services of competent experts to get us those things which the people desire. Having had these submitted to us, we should pass the necessary legislation. That is the only place where a member of parliament should come into the picture.
For instance, I should like to know the names of the people who have suggested to the government that the ills of industry can be cured by the setting up or establishment of an industrial development bank. If industry want another bank, of course they must have it, if they feel that that will solve their problems. But I want to know which section of industry have petitioned for it. I want to know who have recommended this bank to the government, so that, say four or five years hence, we can highly commend them for their

The Address-Mr. Perley
action if it has proven a success and has benefited industry, or, on the other hand, wreak our vengeance upon them if it has bound industry more strongly to finance. Personally I do not think it is a bank that they want; I think what they need are plenty of customers with plenty of buying power. Industry after this war will be capable of turning out goods in tremendous quantities; yet if the consuming public have no buying power, what purpose will be served by turning out so much goods?
Lord Melchett said, just a short time ago:
The problem of the modern world is to provide the population with mass purchasing power to absorb the output of mass production. This lies within the field of finance.
So much for the industrial development bank.
We are to be asked to give our approval to a national health insurance scheme. If it means the sort of thing which the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) complained about a few days ago, I want none of it. If it means the denial of the right of a citizen to engage the services of a chiropractor, an osteopath, or any individual who can relieve suffering and pain, I do not want to have anything to do with it. If it means the denial of the right of the citizen to embrace the philosophical teachings of Christian Science, then, again, I do not want anything to do with it. In other words, if it in any way curtails the freedom of the individual and substitutes an enslavement to bureaucratic regimentation, we shall be better without it.
A few words on family allowances. Here we have a direct admission on the part of the dominion government that industry does not distribute through wages, salary and dividends, sufficient buying power to the consuming public to purchase total production.
Here we have a government endorsing Major Douglas's theory without giving credit where credit is due. If we admit that there is a deficiency of purchasing power inherent in the system, in my judgment we should extend this plan to give to every Canadian citizen sufficient buying power to provide for him and for his family the bare necessities of life. Stuart Chase said recently:
Steadily, reluctantly, even kicking and screaming. western civilization is being driven to the hitherto abhorrent notion that the consumer must be furnished with purchasing power whether he works or not.
That is a very important admission on the part of a man who has held orthodox views for so many years.
In conclusion, I want to say a word to the post-war international planners who are springing up like mushrooms all over the country.
One of the most picturesque figures in all biblical history was that wise old patriarch Solomon, king of Israel. In his day he was pestered with planners, until in a fit of anger he turned to them and said, "The eyes of a fool are in the ends of the earth". I think that might be fittingly applied to the international planners of our day. We should wish our friends of the Soviet Union, China, France, Norway, Belgium, Holland and all other countries, success in reconstruction and reestablishment, of their countries, but we ourselves should get on with the immediate task of solving our own problems at home. Haakon Lie, secretary of the Norwegian Federation of Labour, speaking recently to the Wellesley Institute for Social Progress, said:
We do not want any army of occupation. We can administer our own affairs. We can buy what we need from Britain and America. All we want is our freedom. You can educate your administrators and send them over with the best will in the world, but in a short time they will be as much disliked as the German administrators.
That is something for our meddlesome planners to ponder. I feel quite sure in my own mind that there is a very rude awakening coming to those individuals when the "cease fire" sounds and our young men return from overseas.
I see my time has gone, Mr. Speaker, and there still remain such important questions as agriculture, old age pensions, housing, and so on. They are all big questions, and when they are under discussion in this house I shall have something to say in respect to them. I do want to say, however, that each of these questions is capable of a simple solution. The old axiom "there are none so blind as those who will not see" applies most fittingly to our present administrators. Will it take a revolution to shake them from their complacency?

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in this discussion. I was prepared to accept the suggestion of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) who, in moving his amendment, spoke briefly and said that in his opinion there should be few speeches on the address, that we should wait until the legislation was brought down and we knew what it was all about. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) accepted that suggestion and also spoke briefly, taking only about twenty minutes to deal with general matters before going on to read his statement in regard to the speech by Lord Halifax. It seemed to me that, since the speech from the throne was not very definite, we should wait until we had the actual legislation and then get on with the business

The Address-Mr. Perley

of the country. After listening to the political speech delivered yesterday by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), however, in which he referred to Liberal policies and to the floor prices on agricultural products, I came to the conclusion that I should say a few words at this stage.
May I say quite frankly at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that my first concern is the winning of the war. To my mind that is our most important problem, and the only thing that matters now. Having said that, however, I want to repeat what I said last session, that [ have no apology to offer for having supported certain measures brought down by this government since the beginning of the war, when I thought those measures were in the interest of Canada's war effort. Neither have I an apology to offer for having on occasion criticized this government, I hope constructively, when I thought such criticism would also help the war effort.
When I looked over the speech from the throne point by point, as was suggested by the leader of the opposition, I had to agree with him that most of the legislation there suggested was taken from the platform drawn up by the Progressive Conservative party at Winnipeg in December, 1942. But even at that the Progressive Conservative .party is by uo means stranded,, for there is much remaining in that platform which the government could well adopt and much that the people of Canada will approve when they have a chance to express themselves at the next general election.

the government will agree that I made the suggestions before they thought of them.
Yesterday we listened to two able speeches, delivered with great energy and force, by the 
hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) and the Minister of Agriculture. It developed into a real bout. I am not going to get mixed up in any of their little differences; I am not even going to suggest that I might act as referee, because each scored so many points that it might be a little difficult to say who won. I noticed, however, that each took many of his points from the Progressive Conservative party. The minister took credit, in a forceful way, for the policy of floor prices. In doing that he referred to the fact that the first person to establish floor prices in Canada with respect to the marketing of grain was Right Hon. R. B. Bennett in 1935. This is what the minister said:
My hon. friends opposite say that floor prices came from John Bracken.
Hear, hear; they did.
They forget that we had a floor price under butter in 1938. They forget that we had a floor price under hogs and cheese in 1939-40. They forget that we had a floor price-their own party put a floor price, if you like to go back-of 871 cents under wheat when Mr. Bennett was in power, but they have dropped the name of his party. We have put floor prices all the way from 70 cents to $1.25.
Then he goes on to say that on October 15 the Prime Minister made a statement with respect to floor prices. The minister's memory is not good. The statement made in October was made about a year after the Winnipeg convention, where the principle of an initial floor price was established and put into our policy. Then the minister mentioned the different prices-the initial price, the parity price, and the floor price-and said they were all practically the same, namely, floor prices. When the minister made reference to all these prices I was surprised that his memory was so short. He did not mention all the names pertaining to prices, because he and his parti' were responsible in the fall of 1935 and the beginning of 1936 for establishing what was termed a fire sale price. It will be recalled that following the election, Mr. McFarland was thrown out and Mr. Mclvor took office. It was at that time that a fire sale price was established in an effort to dispose of surplus wheat, which later proved to be a blessing in disguise. They tried to sell that wheat at fire sale prices, offering it in large quantities which the market could not absorb. The minister forgot to mention that yesterday.
The minister then reviewed the situation with respect to prices in 1937, 1938 and 1939, down to the present time. I am not going to go into detail on that matter. I shall say only that it was not very long before the Canadian Wheat Board Act, passed by Mr. Bennett's government in 1935, was set aside by what was

The Address-Mr. Perley
described by the late Hon. Mr. Motherwell as an illegal order in council. Hon. members know what happened. After the fire sale price had been established, in an effort to dispose of the wheat, the price changed; it went up until in 1937 it reached $1.47. Then the act was brought into operation again, and hon. members know the record from that time. As the minister said yesterday, we had a floor price of 70 cents, and then floor prices of 80 cents and 90 cents, down the line. The minister yesterday tried to take credit for the price at $1.25, but we shall have something to say about that later on.
It is hardly necessary, for me to say anything respecting my own stand in these matters. I think every hon. member knows where I stand in regard to prices, and particularly grain prices, which were under discussion yesterday. In 1938, after the fiasco of the fire sale price, I proposed in the house a policy which amounted to a floor price, to be effective not only from year to year, but over a ten-year period. After setting out the circumstances and conditions in connection with marketing I suggested, in 1938, that the government should authorize the board to fix a minimum price of a dollar per bushel for a period of not less than ten years. I mentioned further on that occasion that coarse grains should be brought under the operation of the board, and that a fixed minimum, or, if you like, a floor price, should be placed on coarse grains of export grades. So, who was practically the first to suggest floor prices in the house? On the occasion on which I made.the suggestion in the house we had discussion in our caucus, and I had the support of every hon. member there present for the policy I advanced. We discussed it, and in the main that was the policy of our party.

I was at the Progressive Conservative convention at Winnipeg when we adopted that policy in a plank providing for floor prices. The policy was adopted by the party as a whole on that occasion. The orders of the day in each session from 1940 will show a resolution in my name, asking for a parity price and a minimum price with participation certificates. I say therefore that my record in that respect has been consistent.
Last fall, when the price of $1.25 was announced, in my effort to be fair, as I try to be in all cases, I wrote to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) and complimented him upon his action in setting that price. In my letter I expressed regret that it had not been done sooner. I pointed 100-22i
out that the minister could have taken similar action in March, at the latest in July. It will be recalled that in March he had announced the policy that the 1943 price was to remain at 90 cents. Then in July, having in mind the circumstances surrounding marketing in western Canada, the United States and Europe, I asked the minister to reconsider his policy and to advance the price by at least twenty cents. He replied that he could not do so.
It is of interest to note that when the price was set at $1.25 I had made a motion in the committee on agriculture, in addition to my resolution on the order paper which, because it was private members' business, could not be reached. But on July 16 in the committee on agriculture I made practically the same motion which had stood in my name on the order paper. My motion in committee asked the government to consider increasing the price by twenty cents to $1.10. The committee's report states:
This committee recommends that in view of the changed market conditions the wheat [DOT]committee of the [DOT] cabinet should authorize the initial payment of wheat being increased to $1.10 a bushel basis No. 1 Northern at Fort William, instead of the present 90 cents paid by the Canadian Wheat Board, and the Wheat Board Act should be amended to permit this higher payment, at the present session.
The motion was made on the 16th, and it was ruled out of order on the 19th. When the committee met on the 19th the chairman announced that he had consulted with you, sir, and I believe also with the Clerk of the House, and he then ruled my motion out of order on the ground that it would involve the expenditure of public money. It is interesting to note that having ruled that out on July 19, they proceeded in September to adopt the principle. They even went a little further, for which I am glad.	-
There is another thing about which I am quite pleased. On that same day I moved, as will be seen from the records of the agriculture committee, as follows:
This committee recommends that the government should authorize the Canadian Wheat Board to handle all oats and1 barley on a pooling basis according to grade, with initial price not less than the established ceiling price.
They struck out the words "with initial price not less than the established ceiling price" and then adopted the motion. It is interesting to note that within two weeks they passed an order in council which was my original motion almost word for word. When that motion was put to a vote in the committee only the Conservative members and the C.C.F. members voted for it. It is interesting to note, too, that they have adopted some of my suggestions in that respect.
The Address-Mr. Perley

The farmers have done their part, and all they want is a square deal. They have done everything that has been asked of them in the way of producing products of all kinds. They have helped as much as any other class of our people to finance this war. I am proud to say that the agricultural districts in my constituency have gone over the top early in every victory loan campaign. They have done their duty in many respects and, as I say, all they want is a square deal and an adequate Teturn for their labour.
They also want some controls with respect to our marketing system. The government proposes to establish floor prices, I trust that these prices will not be lower than the ceiling prices now prevailing. There should be participation certificates and the wheat board should be given the necessary control in order to carry out orderly marketing. As has been suggested already, I am firmly of the opinion that the Minister of Agriculture should set up a board of live stock commissioners. If that board had the proper agricultural representation-no one knows better what should be done for the farmer than the man who is actually in the business-it would prove of great help to the minister.
Within the last two or three days questions have been asked by the leader of the Social Credit party and others in this house with respect to the marketing of beef, live stock and so on. This goes to show that conditions are not satisfactory. I shall not take the time now to go into this in detail, but I think the minister would he well advised to consider some of the suggestions that have been made. The western beef producers are dissatisfied, as are the hog producers. I should like to quote from the Regina Leader-Post of January 26, 1944. This is the mouthpiece of the Liberal government and the Minister of Agriculture in Saskatchewan. It says:
Returns for hogs are the lowest since 1938 and the bonus will only put the net return to where it was in 1942.
That shows that his own organ is not very well satisfied. The government should give more attention to what agricultural and cooperative organizations have to say. These organizations are. playing a most important part in the affairs of this country. The federation of agriculture is well organized, and it represents every branch of the agricultural industry.
I said a moment ago that I hoped the floor prices would be set at a level comparable to what the farmer has to pay for the things he consumes, comparable to the prices now being

received in the United States, and they should be set for a term of not less than five to ten years.
There are other suggestions I could make with regard to marketing and agricultural questions with which I am familiar, but I shall not take the time now. There will be an occasion later on. The chief whip of the Liberal party laughs. We shall have something to say on these matters. All the government has to do is to bring down its measures and' we will dissect them. I am generally on the job, and I think I shall be able to give him something to laugh about later on.
There are many matters forecast in the speech from the throne, most of which have been discussed during this debate. I refer to rehabilitation, social security, man-power on the farm, and other labour problems. With respect to social security I shall say just one word. If you want to solve that problem, if you want to'provide security for all the people of Canada on a proper basis, all you need to do is to enact measures that will provide employment for all.
I am going to make one or two suggestions. The government should1 adopt measures to put the four basic industries of Canada on a proper footing. First, there is agriculture with its subsidiary industries of milling, baking and so on. Then there is the lumber industry, with the different forest products. Then there is the mining of minerals, with which would be associated the production of hydro-electric power. And there is the fishing industry. If these four industries are put on a proper basis, every secondary industry will fall in line. They are our four chief industries, and if proper consideration is given to them our difficulties with respect to labour and other problems will be taken care of. I do not intend to gq into the details of what should be done with each industry; there will be another time to discuss these matters.
I regret that the Minister of Agriculture is not in his seat at the moment. I noticed he was here yesterday; it may be that it takes a speaker like the hon. member of Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) to bring him into the chamber. I listened with close attention, as I always do, to what he said yesterday. He made a speech with some punch in it. He tried to convince the members of this house that the present government of which he is a member nad implemented1 the policies laid down from time to time in the different platforms of the Liberal party, and I was surprised to hear the minister take credit to the government for the fact that the employment situation to-day is more or less satisfactory. He sought to leave the impression on the. house and, through Hansard,

The Address-Mr. Perley
with the people of this country, that the . alleged policies of the Liberal party were responsible for the present lack of unemployment. I use the word "alleged" advisedly, because I doubt if there are many people in Canada who have the remotest idea of what the Liberal policies are; they have been changing with such frequency that no one can keep track of them.
