The credit for our larger domestic and foreign trade, to which the Minister of Agriculture referred, cannot be given to this government. Every man in Canada knows that our expanded foreign trade and our enlarged domestic trade is due to the producers in Canada, who are the ones, and the only ones, who should get the credit.
The Minister of Agriculture yesterday, in his little bout with the hon. member for Weyburn, devoted a lot of time to socialists and socialism. I said at the outset that I am not going to assume the role of referee between them.
I will content myself by saying that I do not think the people of Canada are ready for complete socialism. The failure of the Liberal government to solve the economic problems of Canada before the war, despite the ample opportunity they had to do so, and the "feeling in the minds of the people that they would not be able to solve the problems of the after-the-war period, was responsible, .1 think, for the adverse vote which the government received in the by-elections that have taken place in recent months throughout Canada. This was the only opportunity that the people of Canada have had since war broke out of expressing themselves; and how did they do it? Evidently they had concluded that the government was not responsible for the prosperity of which the Minister of Agriculture spoke yesterday.
I have one complaint to make in conclusion, and it is this, that the government, which boast now of setting a floor price of SI.25 for wheat, did not do it earlier. They announced their wheat policy in March of last year, when they said there would be no change in price for the 1943 crop. I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce in July of last year whether he would not reconsider the government's wheat policy, but to no effect. The government did not take action until September 21, when a great deal of our wheat had been marketed under the first quota -because with the present system of harvesting in western Canada, where combines are used, a lot of wheat is marketed in August and September. The open market price at that time was considerably over 90 cents, and many farmers, taking the government at their word that there wouid be no change in policy, sold their wheat at the open market price. I myself took the minister at his word and sold a considerable amount of wheat on the 1st of September. If I had held it a few days I would have got a better price, but I took the minister at his word and sold a considerable portion of my wheat at. the open market price. I think the farmer should receive a proper settlement for the wheat he sold during that period from August 1 to September 21. The settlement on the basis of the spread is not good enough, and the farmers will not forget it. I got three-quarters of a cent in the spread between the price on the day I sold my wheat and the price on the day the government set a floor of S1.25. I think something should be done even now about that. I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce when we may expect a statement from him with reference to the amount of wheat taken over by the board, the price paid for it, and the profit made. I think we should have that statement before long.
The Address

Mr. Coldwell

Much has been said in this debate about the price of hogs and other products, and I listened to the Minister of Agriculture yesterday trying to square himself or get himself out of the mess in which he apparently finds himself because undoubtedly there is a lot of dissatisfaction with the government's agricultural policy. It reminds me of the pictures of a boy riding a donkey. In one picture you see him riding facing one way, and in the next picture you see him facing in the opposite direction, so that you cannot tell where he is going. The minister has been riding the hog both ways and has got into trouble. We shall have something to say later on this question, *but I trust that this debate will close soon and that we shall get down to the business of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I had not intended to participate further in this debate, but yesterday's remarks of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) have prompted me to do so. First, however, let me say that I agree with very much of what the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Perley) has said, though I would remind him that if we are entering into a competition to see who first suggested parity prices or floor prices we should look to many of the farm organizations in the west. I believe that as a matter of fact the movement for which I speak to-day was the first movement to incorporate such a plank in a political platform. I have before me our Regina manifesto of 1933 and I find in it clause 4 under agriculture:
The encouragement of producers' and consumers' cooperatives; the restoration and maintenance of an equitable relationship between prices of agricultural products and those of other commodities and farm services.
As long ago as 1933 we were urging and advocating that form of price level guarantee.
Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture made a political speech in the course of which he saw fit to make a number of statements that were inaccurate and that misrepresented the viewpoint and the basis of the movement which the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group represents in this house. He attacked particularly my hon. friend the member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) and chided him because he had not yet found a seat in the provincial house at Regina. Well, we must remind the minister, as we did yesterday, that for almost two years one provincial seat has been vacant in the province of Saskatchewan and that since July last three others have been vacant, one of them a seat formerly occupied by the present hon. member for Humboldt in this house (Mr. Burton), a seat occupied by a C.C.F. member. At any time the government 
of Saskatchewan could have opened one of these seats, and I am quite sure the hon. member for Weyburn would have been glad to seize the opportunity and attempt to enter the Saskatchewan house at Regina.
I presume the minister is alarmed because the political machine in Saskatchewan, upon which he has relied so long, has shown signs of breaking down. In the Humboldt by-election we had that machine in full force in the constituency. The minister was there himself, having left parliament before this house rose in July, to supervise that campaign, and he gathered round him the old cohorts of the Saskatchewan Liberal machine. And let me say that there has been no more devastating machine in the democratic world than that organized by the Minister of Agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan. Let me tell the house that employees of the federal government were there in force with cars belonging to the Dominion of Canada. We made a check of them. I have before me only a partial list of some of the cars that were present during the time I myself was in that constituency. I saw some of	them parked
outside the hotel where I was staying, which also happened to be the headquarters of the Liberal party. We took a number of car numbers; all the following are Saskatchewan licence numbers of the dominion Department of Agriculture, P.FjR.A. Regina.
No. 20475	No.	20444No. 20471	No.	20452No. 20474	No.	2045S

They must have been a fleet of jeeps.
Mr. COLDWELL; No. They were not jeeps. Some were fine modem cdrs, including one fine maroon car which I am told the minister himself drove on one occasion to attend a political appointment. Who paid for the gas and upkeep of the cars? The people of Canada. But the political machine is so brazen in the province of Saskatchewan that it dared to do this sort of thing in the midst of a by-election. And so, when the minister talks about regimentation, let me remind the house that no other province in this dominion, at any time, has been regimented in poverty by a political machine to the extent that Saskatchewan was regimented during the depression years. Unless you were a member of the Liberal party or had a recommendation from that party you found it difficult to get relief work.
That is untrue.

You found it difficult to get anything at all. I know the facts.

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
That statement is not correct.

This statement is just as correct as the statement about the cars, the basis of which statement I witnessed with my own eyes. No other province has been controlled to the extent that Saskatchewan has been under the regime of the present Minister of Agriculture. And so I say that when the time comes wre shall want to know what the expense accounts were of those gentlemen who were in the town of Humboldt during the byelection between the middle of July and the 9th of August when the minister himself was there.
The minister took particular credit yesterday for the fact, as he claimed, that the province of Saskatchewan had on the statute books, in principle at least, everything that was to be found in the Beveridge report. Well, they may be there in principle, but there are thousands of square miles of territory in Saskatchewan without adequate social services upon which a community must depend at this time, particularly medical services, as the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie well knows. And as for taking credit for the municipal doctors and other cooperative medical facilities in that province, those of us who know their history know that health organizations arose out of the needs of the people and were organized first by the people themselves and then the government came along with its legislation.
As for social services like education, there were schools without teachers, teachers working in the province for $350 a year and not getting paid during long years of Liberal administration in that province, so that when the minister rises in this house and gives us the province of Saskatchewan as an example of what the Liberal government would do, I say heaven save us from a Liberal government in the dominion who would follow that example.
We learned yesterday too that the government took credit for the improved conditions when the war broke out or prior to the breaking out of the war. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who has just taken his seat, gave the house the reason for the improved trade conditions immediately prior to the war. Canada was assisting in the rearming of the aggressor nations. Session after session we and others in this house rose and pointed out the exports of nickel, exports of aluminum, exports of copper, exports of scrapiron that were going in an ever-increasing stream to the present enemy nations, particularly to Japan. We know that one large mine, the Granby mine, in the province of British Columbia, was permitted for several years to send to Japan all its output of copper concentrates. We know that well into 1940, long after we were at war with the German reich, this government was permitting the export of nickel, copper, aluminum and scrapiron to Japan, in order that she might rearm herself.

Part of which went to
Russia.

That, let me add, was
the cause, to some extent at least, of the increased trade figures which were presented to this house at that time. So I say that the government can find very little comfort in the statements made in that regard.
Then, of course, he twitted us with socialism. I am going to say something about that in a moment. But let me point out here that no government could have regimented our young men and women more thoroughly than the Liberal government regimented them in those years before the war. They regimented them in poverty and want. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perleyl made a statement regarding the condition in 1939 which was disputed by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross). If he will look up the relief figures for 1939 he will find that at one time in that year there were nearly one million people in this country on relief, and four hundred thousand registered unemployed. I say that no government in any country could have regimented in poverty and1 want the people to a greater extent than the present government which sits opposite.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Those were world conditions.

Five dollars a month on a farm and three cents for a meal. The minister yesterday denied that men were riding the rods during the regime of this government. True, they were riding the rods in 1933, 1934 and 1935, when Mr. Bennett was in power, but they were also riding the rods in 1939, 1938, 1937, 1936. I remember vividly one incident which occurred under this roof in 1939. About this time of the year, early in February, there came into the office of my friend, Grant MacNeil, half a dozen young men, who were the vanguard of a number who had ridden the rods into this city, having been sent first of all from Vancouver to the province of Ontario. They came in homeless, foodless and cold. We got in touch with the then Minister of Labour, one of the kindliest men who have ever sat in this house, the late Hon. Norman Rogers. Mr. Rogers said: "My department can do nothing for them. We make grants to the provinces." Grant MacNeil got in touch with the province of Ontario: "We can do nothing
The Address-Mr. Coldwell

for them; they have not been in Ontario a year." Mr. MacNeil phoned the civic authorities: "We can do nothing for them; they have not been in the city three months." And a Liberal member in this house at that time rose in his place and described those two or three hundred men who were here the following week as-what? "Bums, toughs, yaps, ne'er-do-wells." And they drifted away. After the war broke out, in September, 1939, I happened to be walking down O'Connor street, away from this house. As I passed a recruiting station, or what I supposed was a recruiting station, for there were a lot of young men around there, I heard someone say, "There is Mr. Coldwell." I turned to him and asked, "What part of Saskatchewan are you from?" He said, "I am not from Saskatchewan; I am one of the boys who were in Mr. MacNeil's office in February. I have joined up." I shook hands with him and I wished him good luck. That boy, who could not get a fifteen-cent meal from the Dominion of Canada in February, who was a "bum," "spineless," and all the rest of it, according to a Liberal member of this house, in February, joined up. What did he get? He got a good suit of clothes, a good warm overcoat, good underwear, socks and shoes, three good meals a day, a ticket to the Y.M.C.A.-and socialized1 medicine thrown in with it, as my hon. friends -remind me. These boys were "no good" in peace, but when war came they became necessary for our defence. But the government, which is yet in power, sat unmoved and did nothing to relieve their distress. They left them to ride the rods.
They waited on world trade!

Yes; as my hon. friend says, they waited on world trade. Yesterday the minister spoke to us of world trade. I believe in world trade; you export in order to import the goods which you need. But my hon. friends dare to tell me that world trade was the solution in this country when there were a million people on relief and four hundred thousand unemployed? In the city in which I live, and which is probably one of the best in the dominion in respect of relief so far as amounts go, three meals a day at three cents a meal was the average family allowance. And my hon. friends tell me that we ought to have exported more food? We say we ought to have fed some of the people. And we have reaped the nemesis since. I remember a former minister, the Hon. Mr. Thoi'son, rising in this house and telling us that forty-four per cent of the young men who had volunteered and been examined were turned down on account of physical 
unfitness. That was the result of the years when this government was in power. And then they say, "Put the C.C.F. in power and they will regiment you." We want to free men from that kind of regimentation, and if we ever get the opportunity, as we shall, we shall do it.
The minister said that we sent emissaries to national socialist countries to see what they were doing there. Where did he get his information from? We sent no emissaries. When we asked him whom he had in mind he named Major George H. Williams-a man who to-day is serving in the Canadian army overseas-as having been an emissary to a national socialist country to come back to teach this country national socialism, the thing we are fighting against. Major Williams is not only serving in this war but took part and was wounded in the war of 1914-18. Where did he go? He went to Russia. Did we send him there? No, we did not send him there. He was sent there by the farmers of Saskatchewan to study the agricultural problems of that country and how they were going to meet them, and what effect they might have in the future on the agricultural economy of our own country, and particularly of our prairie provinces. That is why Mr. Williams went to Russia. A few year's ago, of course, even three or four years ago, hon. members would rise in their places and call us communists. "Russia" was thrown at us. Now, of course, Russia is our ally, communism is a bit more popular, and so they turn around and call us national socialists.
They have to have something.

Yes, they have to have something. But let me tell them that calling names will not meet argument, and calling names of that description will do them more harm than it will do us. As far as we are concerned we are the most democratically based political party in this country, indeed probably anywhere in the world; and our democratic associations are recognized in other countries.
May I interject this personal experience. I know I am the only member of this house ever to be invited to sit in at a labour party caucus in Great Britain, as I did on November 10, 1941, with Clement Attlee, Ernest Bevin, Herbert Morrison, A. V. Alexander and the other men who to-day are giving leadership in this struggle against national socialism but who hold to exactly the same kind of democratic socialist principles that we in this group hold to in this country; and that is recognized. So that I do not think that such stupidity

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
is going to carry any weight in this country; and to vilify a man who is serving his country overseas at this time is almost beneath contempt.
The minister said he was quoting from a book. What book? Well, at the conclusion of his remarks he held up this book, "Make This Your Canada." I would recommend that all hon. members read it; then perhaps they may know something more about the C.C.F. and be prepared to discuss it intelligently. But later on, when the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) was speaking, I noticed that the minister interjected that the book was "Social Planning for Canada." We did not write or produce that book. It was written by a group of men associated with the League for Social Reconstruction of which, if I am not misinformed, some hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side of the house were members in the early nineteen-thirties.
Who would they be?

Well, I am not going to say, but I will ask this. Who were the authors of that book? It was written by a group of brilliant young men, one of whom, Doctor Leonard Marsh, is in an advisory capacity to one of the most important committees this government has set up, the social security committee. Indeed, he drafted their plan for them. Another one, Graham Spry, is now the personal assistant to Right Hon. Stafford Cripps in Britain. Some national socialists, aren't they, people of that description? Page the Minister of Agriculture, somebody says. I' should say so.
Where is he?
Probably busy.

Probably
scared.
Of what?

Yesterday I think this house took the measure of the minister in the kind of speech he made, when he tried to suggest that people like those I have mentioned were national socialists. If he had called anyone in this house a national socialist then he should have gone further and laid a charge with the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and had that person interned, because we are at war with national socialism. Therefore when we examine a speech like the one made yesterday, so full of misrepresentations, it makes us wonder just what idea the minister has of the quality of thinking of our Canadian people.
A few moments ago I said that ours was the most truly democratic movement in Canada, and it is. We are the only political party
organized in this manner. Back in our constituencies and throughout the country there are literally hundreds of clubs of ordinary, plain people meeting together regularly, studying the economic and social conditions of the country in which we live, formulating their ideas, putting them into resolution form, sending them to our constituency conventions, then up to the provincial conventions, held every year, and finally to the national convention, held every two years, to which the delegates are elected by the people. That is not like a Liberal convention held once every twenty-five years. The minister said yesterday, "Oh, yes; they held a meeting in Regina behind closed doors." Every political party holds its caucuses behind closed doors. The meeting referred to was a meeting of elected representatives, in the main, federal and provincial, in order to sort out some of the problems that confront both parliament and legislature. We thought that was a real contribution to the welfare of Canada at this time. What about the Liberal party? It has not had a national convention for twenty-five years. Oh, yes, they had a meeting last September. I happened to come into the House of Commons at the time a meeting was being held; and the meeting place, the railway committee room, was veiy carefully guarded by police. We did not have any police at our meeting in Regina; we did not need them.
That was not a meeting at all.
It was a caucus, and ours was a caucus, too. Then a meeting of the Liberal federation was held at the Chateau Laurier. Was the press admitted?
Part of the time.
Does anybody know what was adopted at that Liberal federation meeting?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Yes; it was given to the press.

No, it was not. We
were told that we would hear what the Liberal federation had decided when the programme of the government was brought down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: No.

Oh, yes, we were; I
can produce the press clippings to that effect. So that I say to the minister, let him beware when he hurls stones at some of the other people in this house, that he does not live in a very thin glass-house himself, for some stones may be hurled back at him.
I say we are a democratic political movement based on the people themselves. I have
The Address-Mr. Coldwell

no preemption of the position I hold to-day. I am elected or reelected every time there is a national convention, unless they wish to replace me by someone else. That is mass control; that is control by the people; that is democratic control, if you will, and we intend to keep it that way. I noticed, too, that the minister said he wanted to agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) the other evening. I am prepared to place the record of this movement in pre-war international affairs beside the record of any other party in this house. We are not provincial isolationists, like my hon. friends to the left; nor do we dodge every issue that comes along, like my hon. friends to the immediate right; nor do we delay issues, like the government.
You were getting along pretty well until now.

Well, I should like Mr. Bracken to make a statement on some important matters. During pre-war years we demanded collective security, and the carrying out of league obligations. From 1931 right up to the outbreak of war we condemned the support that was being given by powerful interests throughout the world to Germany, Italy and Japan. We demanded that that cease. We denounced Mussolini when others were praising him, when they were coming back from Italy, as Colonel George Drew did, telling us that Mussolini was a wonderful man, that he had drained the marshes, made the trains run on time, and so on, and so on. We.were denouncing the same Mussolini.
It is great to be perfect.

And we were denouncing Hitler all through those years, even when we were told that if Hitler had only stopped at a certain point he would have been, a pretty good man. I remember that being said by the late Doctor Manion, the then leader of the Conservative party in the house. And we denounced Hitler, too, when some of our Liberal friends in Saskatchewan were addressing meetings in swastika-decorated halls-yes, in swastika-decorated halls.
True, we did demand disarmament as had oeen agreed to in the league covenant. We did denounce wars which were fought for economic interests, imperialist interests, and purely for trade and for commerce. And during those years we drew attention again and again to the preponderance of league power, if we cared to use it, for the preservation of peace.
With respect to Munich I am prepared to put the record of this movement opposite that of any other group in Canada. When Munich came in September 1938, I telegraphed the League of Nations Society in Canada, a mem-

ber of whose executive I was at the time, and stated this:
Chemaimis, B.C., Sept. 30, 1938.
European situation direct result of desertion of league covenant and collective security by great powers. Believe shameful partition of Czechoslovakia could have been prevented and war averted if league nations had resisted unitedly.
Result of fascist aggression demonstrates peril of small nations which rely on pledges of great powers and the honour of their reactionary politicians.
Urge world-wide campaign to revitalize league to prevent further aggression so clearly foreshadowed by success of Hitler's threat to world peace and human brotherhood.
That was my view at the time of Munich.
What was the view of the leader of the Liberal party? I shall read it, and place it on the record. This communication is dated at Ottawa, September 29, 1938, and states:
The Right Honourable Neville Chamberlain, P.C., M.P., Prime Minister of Great Britain, 10 Downing street, London, England.
The heart of Canada is rejoicing to-night' at the success which has crowned your unremitting efforts for peace. May I convey to you the warm congratulations of the Canadian people, and with them, an expression of their gratitude, which is felt from one end of the dominion to the other. My colleagues in the government join with me in unbounded admiration at the service you have rendered mankind. Your achievements in the past month alone will ensure you an abiding and illustrious place among the great conciliators whom the United Kingdom the British commonwealtn of nations and the whole world will continue to honour. On the very brink of chaos, with passions flaming, and armies marching, the voice of reason has found a way out of the conflict which no people in their heart desired, but none seemed able to avert. A turning point in the world's history will be reached if, as we hope, to-night's agreement means a halt to the mad race of arms, and a new start in building the partnership of all peoples. May you have health and strength to carry your great work to its completion.
W. L. Mackenzie King.
That was signed by the present Prime Minister.
I did not rejoice in the autumn of 1938 when the gallant little nation of Czechoslovakia was sacrificed. Now we know that the sacrifice of that nation had tremendous and serious effects on the future of the world. Doctor Riptka, under-secretary of state for foreign affairs in the Czechoslovakian government now in London has published in his book, "Munich and After", the whole story of the Munich agreement, together with the Czech documents. Among them one will find, if he reads the book, that they had a firm commitment from Russia that if France marched, and Britain marched with her for the protection of Czechoslovakia, Russia would march, too. And because of the deep distrust placed in the

The Address-Mr. Crerar
hearts of the rulers of Russia at that time, a year later we have the Stalin-Hitler pact, and the way cleared for the outbreak of war in which, for a time, the British Commonwealth and Empire stood alone.
And so I say to-day I am not ashamed of the part we played before the war. In that connection, Mr. Speaker, I might refer to a speech I made on September 26, 1938, in the city of Victoria. I have the report of that speech as it appears in the Regina Leader-Post on September 27 of that year. This is a Canadian Press dispatch from Victoria, British Columbia.
What year was that?
It is important to have the right date.

It states:
"Believing that Prime Minister Chamberlain has been forced into the present situation, if war conies we must give whatever assistance we can," he said.
"As a fundamental of participation, Canada must be organized economically to render maximum assistance. All essential industries muBt be placed under national control and profiteering of all kinds eliminated completely."
You see, at that time I thought perhaps the great powers might honour their obligations. The report continues:
"Canada must decide what her best contribution can be. To my mind this is economic. There probably is insufficient national unity to organize a large expeditionary force."
Practically everybody agreed with that. Speaking in this house in March, 1939, six months later, the Prime Minister made the statement that in his opinion we would never again send a force overseas, and that it was unthinkable that every twenty-five years or so we should send our youth across the seas. That was pretty much the general opinion at that time-that it would be difficult to organize and dispatch an expeditionary force.
Then the report goes on to say:
"The present situation arose from conditions that prevailed, prior to the great war," the C.C.F. member said.
"We desire not national rearmament but collective security," continued Mr. Coldwell.
"In other words, we hold that peace cannot be maintained by armed alliances. The League of Nations has not failed, but the statesmanship of the great powers has failed.
"To-day humanity seems to reap the whirlwind, whereas collective security properly applied could have prevented this situation.
"We tolerated the Japanese seizure of Manchuria in 1931.
"Having failed to disarm themselves the league powers allowed Hitler to commence arming. In 1936 his remilitarization of the Rhineland was permitted.
"Toward fascist Italy we have pursued a similar policy. Non-intervention policies in Spain in the face of German and Italian aggression strengthened the fascists."
That was my view in September, 1938. And I say quite freely that in September, 1939, with the people who had made the Munich agreement still in power I was afraid -yes, afraid, that we might once again find our boys sacrificed to the people who were in office, and had made the Munich agreement. But when Dunkirk came, when that government was overthrown and was replaced by one which represented the people of Great Britain, one in which we could have more confidence, the situation was different. To-day my own late leader, Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, who is sometimes vilified, has two sons in the armed forces, and my own son is serving in the air force overseas. So let us stop this kind of foolish name-calling and bandying of words. That was all the minister indulged in yesterday. If we stop that sort of thing we should get along with the business of the house and the war. But I am going to add this, that the kind of argument we heard yesterday will be met whenever it is made in this chamber. We are not on the defensive; we are on the offensive. It is the government that has to answer for many things. It is the government that kept the people regimented in starvation during the depression. It is the government that has no plan for the future. We will cooperate to make plans for the future, but when there is misrepresentation or vilification we shall not let that misrepresentation or vilification go unchallenged.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, until the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) rose in the house I had not the slightest intention of taking part in this debate. With what my hon. friend had to say concerning my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), I am not going to deal in my remarks. The Minister of Agriculture has demonstrated on more than one occasion that he can look after himself, and I have no doubt whatever that he will look after himself so far as the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar are concerned. But it is in connection with the latter part of the speech made by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation that I wish to make a few observations to the house.
If my hon. friend seeks to give the impression to this country that his record and the record of the C.C.F. so far as the war is concerned, so far as the conditions leading up to the war are concerned, are as rosy and fine
The Address-Mr. Crerar

and wholesome as he indicates, then he has a big job on his hands. My hon. friend states the position he took at the time of Munich. If Great Britain and France at the time of Munich had gone to war with Germany in support of Czechoslovakia, I put this question to my hon. friend and to those who sit behind him: Would they have favoured Canada's participating in that fight to crush the tyranny of Germany?
I said so in the very speech to which I referred.
If that was the view of my hon. friend, then the position he took when war broke out was an extraordinary position.
I did not trust the governments.
Oh, oh.
My hon. friend gives a very lame reason for not standing unanimously with parliament in support of the war when it was declared by Canada in September, 1939.
I did. I voted for it, as did every hon. member of this party except Mr. Woodsworth.

My hon. friend did not
stand for effective participation by Canada in the war.
Yes, I did.

I shall read the record in a moment. He gives us as a reason for his vacillating attitude at that time the fact that he did not trust this government or the Prime Minister of Great Britain. Is a' great national question like that to be decided by the hon. gentleman by his not liking some one who is in a government or at the head of a government?
I have to decide according to my own conscience.
All I have to say is that my hon. friend has quite an extraordinary conscience.
If we are going to talk about consciences, I am not going to take anything of that from my hon. friend.
Order.

I did not interrupt my hon. friend when he was making his speech. I want to go back a little prior to the declaration of war by this parliament, September 9, 1939.

What was the attitude of my hon. friend and those who sit behind him when we were dealing with the defence estimates presented by the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) when he was Minister of Defence in 1936, 1937 and 1938? I have the record here. I shall refer the house to the pages of Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: "Facts are chiels that winna ding."

It was clear to any one
who knew anything about the international situation that the storm clouds throughout the world were rising. When the Minister of Pensions and National Health as Minister of National Defence sought to get a modest increase in the estimates for national defence for Canada, what was the attitude of my hon. friend? I happened to have some notes in my desk which I sent for after my hon. friend rose in his place. The hon. member who leads the C.C.F. party in the House of Commons is reported on page 3203 of Hansard of May 28, 1936-my hon. friend can mark down the page number and check it up-as follows:
. .	. in my opinion a country the size of
Canada, with its diverse peoples and small population, is best defended if we rely upon our weakness physically and our good will as a good world neighbour, rather than attempt to ape the military powers of the European countries.
If my hon. friend's policy had been adopted when war broke out and the Japanese nation had attacked the shores of Canada, as was quite possible, where would we have been in the defence of Canada?
Oil sanctions.

My hon. friend refers to
the shipping of materials to Japan, Germany, Russia and other countries. I am not going to debate that matter at the moment more than to say that it is a difficult and dangerous thing in peace time for a government of one country to throw down a challenge to the government of another country in the way suggested by my hon. friend. There is another delightful gem of the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) who took part in this debate yesterday. This was delivered when we were endeavouring to get a modest increase-let me repeat that-in the defence estimates in 1937.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Far too modest.

Far too modest, the Minister of Pensions and National Health suggests, in the light of events that later occurred.

The Address-Mr. Crerar
When on February 19, 1937, we were endeavouring to get this modest increase in the defence estimates the hon. member for Weyburn delivered himself of this gem, and I invite the attention of the house while I read it:
Against whom are we arming? What potential aggressor is more aggressive to-day? Oh,
I know that bogeymen have been trotted out in this chamber. It has been suggested that it might be Italy, it might be Germany, it might be Japan!
Finish the paragraph.
I do not need to.
You dare not finish it and give the context.
I did not interrupt my hon. friend yesterday when he was speaking, and I ask him to refrain from interrupting me.
That is typical.

I rise to a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The minister, without a Hansard before him rises and quotes a sentence from my speech without giving the context. He is quoting from page 1063, and I know the rest of that paragraph. I will give it to the minister if he wishes. But I ask him to quote the rest of that paragraph or to withdraw what he has already said.
Oh.
Otherwise it is tantamount to a complete misrepresentation of my remarks.
May I say to my hon. friend that I have had a little too much experience in this house-

Order. The hon. member for Weyburn has raised a point of order with regard to the quotation made by the minister. If the quotation made by the minister is not correct, of course the hon. gentleman will have an opportunity of correcting it. But the minister is making his speech and he is entitled to make it as he sees fit.

The quotation I have
made is a correct quotation from Hansard.
But an incomplete one.

My hon. friend will find nothing in his speech at that time that will water down or qualify the definite statements which he made and which I have quoted.
But there is more than that. In 1937 the hon. gentleman who now leads the C.C.F.
took part in the debate on the defence estimates of that year and made this statement on November 15, at page 888:
Are we in Canada going to join in this mad race without knowing (precisely the policy that underlies the increased estimates upon which we shall shortly have to vote? Our answer in this little group is, of course, no, because we believe that such defence preparations only breed fear, and that hate, which, in turn, is the child of fear.
That was the lofty sentiment expressed by my hon. friend on that occasion. That would have been of very little avail against an armed Germany and an armed Japan, and I say to my hon. friends of the C.C.F. and to this house that if their point of view had been accepted by parliament at that time, not only would there have been no increase in the defence estimates, not only should we have had not even a modest preparation against the dangers that everyone could see were rising, but we would have dropped our defence estimates altogether and would have retired or, as my hon. friend suggested the year before, to defencelessness as our best defence.
We would have had an international policy.

Well, I leave that to my hon. friend.
There was a by-election in Selkirk last August. It did not turn out very well for the government; my hon. friends' candidate won. I have here that candidate's circular and some of his campaign literature in which he said: "If you want to win the war, vote for the C.C.F." My hon. friend nods his head in approval. But what was the position taken by my hon. friend himself when war broke out? The might of Germany then was known. Russia was not then a member of the allied nations fighting Germany because she had a truce, temporary it is true, with Germany, a truce that was uncertain in character. But at that supreme moment, when Britain was threatened as she never had been threatened before in a thousand years of her history, what was the position of my hon. friend and those who sit behind him?
The same as the government's.

When this government
decided to declare war on Germany, my hon. friend made a declaration in this house. I do not wish to deal unkindly with him at all, but it is well known that in his group there were strong differences of opinion. The leader of the party at that time was the late Mr. Woodsworth, for whom I had a very great
342	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
respect, and Mr. Woodsworth took a line in this house different from that taken by my hon. friend because Mr. Woodsworth said that we should not take any part in the war whatever. But my hon. friend made the declaration that our effort should be wholly economic in character and that no forces should be sent overseas. What would have happened to the commonwealth air training plan under that policy? What would have happened to the assistance we have given on the ocean in carrying and convoying supplies to Britain, without which she could not win the war? I say to my hon. friend and to this house and to the country that if my hon. friend's policy had been accepted and adopted by this country at that time Canada would have done nothing toward helping to win this terrible war. So when my hon. friend endeavours to give the impression that his party were the only real patriots at that time-
I never said that-

No, but my hon. friend has criticized everyone else, so what else can we think? I have not the slightest doubt, Mr. Speaker, that when the people of this country get all these facts before them, as they will, they will deal and deal effectively with my hon. friend the leader of the Commonwealth Cooperative Federation and those who sit behind him in this house.

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. This afternoon the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) was permitted to place on the record a statement which he read from a piece of paper and which purported to be an extract from Hansard of a quotation from a speech which I had made. I objected at the time, and I now claim the right, first of all, to point out that the quotation made by the minister was incomplete and therefore incorrect-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No. I was not incorrect.

-and I claim the right to read to the house and to place on the record the statement from Hansard, not from a piece of paper which I hold in my hand but from volume 2 of the session of 1937, February 19, page 1063.	The quotation
follows-

Do I understand that the hon. member claims the right to reply to the Minister of Mines and Resources with regard to a statement which the hon. member declares is incorrect? Do I understand that to be his point of order? The Minister of Mines and Resources is of course the judge of his own speech, and if he makes a quotation from any speech or any document which has a bearing, as in this instance, on what the hon. member said on a former occasion, if the quotation he makes is in the exact terms of the record, he is entitled to make it. If the hon. member thinks and states that he has been incorrectly reported and therefore that what has been said is untrue, he has the right to make a correction. In this instance, however, I understand the hon. member to say, not that he has been incorrectly quoted, but that the whole quotation has not been given and that therefore the meaning which the hon. member intended to convey in the speech in question has been distorted. There is nothing incorrect, nothing untrue, in what the Minister of Mines and Resources has said, and the opportunity may arise when the hon. member for Weyburn will have the right to place on the record his interpretation of the statement made by the minister. On the basis of what the hon. member has now said, however, 1 cannot hold that he is in order.
May I point out that it is not a matter of interpretation-
Order.
I am pointing out-
Order.
I have a right to rise to a question of privilege.

I am of course willing to give as much latitude as possible, but the point of order as stated by the hon. member is not well taken. It is a question as to the correctness or incorrectness of a statement made by the minister and is therefore not a point of order.

My point of order is this: I am not calling in question any statement; the question I am discussing is whether or not the minister was quoting correctly from my statement. He had on his desk not a copy of Hansard but a piece of paper, and I contend that no member in this house has a right to quote from Hansard unless he quotes correctly.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
On a point of order, I have before me a

The Address-Mr. Picard
copy of what the minister said this afternoon and I have also before me a copy of Hansard, and on my honour as a member of the house I say that what the minister said is absolutely correct in every detail.

I must rule against the point raised by the hon. member for Weybum. In the first place, I do not think it is a point of order. If an hon. member wishes to quote in his address any part of a speech he is entitled to do so. Here, however, no point of order is involved, and the hon. member will have to take any opportunity afforded him to place before the house what he intended to convey.
An opportunity to refute political dishonesty.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The dishonesty is over there.

That of course must
necessarily be a matter of opinion.

Anybody rising at this stage of the debate on the address usually starts by saying that he had no intention of speaking but is forced to do so through some intervention in the debate by some other member. I will follow the tradition and say that I did not intend to speak but that tjie sub-amendment proposed by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) and now before us is the reason for my addressing the house to-night.
I do not feel that I should deal with the first three paragraphs of the subamendent because my position on such questions is well known. I have dealt with them on previous occasions and I shall have an opportunity to do so again in the future. But, Mr. Speaker, I represent an entirely rural constituency in the province of Quebec, and as the fourth paragraph in this subamendment reads that the government-
Failed to grant to farmers and fishermen exemption from military service in order to remove from them the vexatious proceedings resulting from the narrow application of the national selective service regulations.	*
I feel I should explain my position.
Even with 'these words in the subamendment I declare at once that I cannot vote for it because I am convinced that the farmers of my province as well as the farmers of all Canada have been treated fairly.
The farmers are not asking for any special law for themselves. The regulations existing at the moment give them all due opportunity to get deferments and to be left to till the soil if they properly present their applications to the different boards organized by the
Department of Labour. The farmers want to be treated as all other good citizens of this country are treated, and they are just as patriotic as other classes in the community. They know that the policy of this government has been to keep in their present occupations all men whose labour is considered essential to the prosecution of the war. In this regard they know that all important industries dealing with the war effort, munition plants, shipbuilding plants, and most of the war industries, have been given the privilege of declaring who, among their men, when they are called, are essential to production. And these men upon the declaration of these industries are given deferment.
The farmers occupy an even better position from the point of view of preferment. In the first year of the application of the mobilization act a farmer had to prove that he was essential on the land in order to obtain deferment. Soon after the plans for agricultural expansion in Canada were brought down the Department of Agriculture realized that, in order to send to Britain and to the other united nations the quota they had agreed to supply, all men occupied in agriculture, farmer-owners, sons of farmers or others engaged in agriculture, were necessary and had to be left to till the soil.
As I stated in this house on two previous occasions, the government realized "that the land is the first element that enters into the question of production and that farming is the primary industry and most essential in carrying on the war, because the best trained men, with the best and most modern equipment, cannot fight on an empty stomach."
From then on the farmers throughout Canada had only to establish their status to get deferment from military service either to work on their own farms or to work on the farms of their fathers, or, if those farms were well enough supplied with labour, to be sent to work as farm hands on farms where there were no sons of an age to work, or where there was lack of man-power.
My experience-and I say again that I represent a constituency 98 per cent rural-is that the farmers are satisfied, and I have ample evidence from letters from my own constituents showing that they recognize that they have been well treated and recognize what has been done by this government, not as a favour to one class of the population, but to ensure adequate production of food for Canada, to be sent to Britain and to be supplied to the United Nations. As I say that they have been well treated I intend, for the sake of the record and although we all know about this, to outline in a few words the
The Address-Mr. Picard

procedure which was followed, and which, when followed, permitted these farmers to remain on the farms if they were bona fide farmers.
The moment these men were called, as every other Canadian citizen coming of age was called, if they were notified that their medical examination classed them in a category where they were callable for service, they had to file a form stating the size of the farm, the quantity of cattle or hogs or other animals that they had; in short, to explain what sort of farm they had and how many people there were on the farm. Immediately that procedure had been followed, the registrar of their district would, if the evidence was suffi-ficient, immediately issue to them a certificate stating that they were deferred until further notice, which meant that unless the enemy landed on Canadian soil they would be left to till the soil and produce the food necessary for our armies.
Those who may not have supplied all the documents necessary to prove to the registrar their good faith, or the necessity of their remaining on their parents' farm, were, if there was enough evidence to show that they had been the larger part of their life on a farm and knew about farming and desired to carry on that kind of work, given deferments of from three to six months; and that limit was not to cause them any trouble, as this amendment might lead us to believe, but to make sure, as the government had to do, that these men would remain and work on the farm for the production of food, and were not trying to get deferment in order to go into industry, as was done under regulations which were in force during the last war.
Our people in good faith produced that evidence, showed it to the registrars or to the courts of inquiry that had authority to revise the decisions of the registrars and, once they showed their good faith, were immediately given deferments. Those who were given three to six months deferments, received further extension from six months to six months, after evidence was produced that they were really on the farms.
Some will say that there were men in the first months of the application of the mobilization act who were called at the time for four months and did not ask for any deferment, as they were willing to go for four months, that they entered the army, and that afterwards the procedure to get them out to go back and till the soil was a little difficult. Well, such cases have happened. I have had some myself in my constituency. I have some that are not yet solved. But most of them have been carefully scrutinized by the army authorities, and I must say that, especially in the last year, there has been a great improve-

ment. When the Department of Agriculture impressed upon national selective service authorities that all the men needed for agricultural production had to be returned to the land whenever the man was not in an operational unit and it could be proved that his father needed him on the farm, and when we presented the case to the military authorities, men who were in the different camps throughout Canada were released for periods of from three to six months for duty on the farms, and some of them had their leave extended for other periods of six months. Furthermore, these agriculturists have even been begged by the government to go into the forests during the months they were not absolutely necessary on the farms and work for lumber companies. This was not done to give preferences to special classes of the population, but in order that they could produce the lumber so much needed for the war effort. As regards most of these cases which at first gave trouble to some hon. members because the men had not applied for deferment and were inducted in the army because they were willing to serve, and whose fathers seeing the production on their land lagging, asked to get them back for a certain period of the year - they have been for the most part redressed. I myself have some cases which have not yet been solved1, of men who are already over one year in the army on the Pacific coast or the Atlantic coast. There may be difficulties in connection with their farms. I say there may be some such cases, but would this house be justified in passing such an amendment merely because in certain cases the circumstances have not been understood by some officers of the Department of National Defence as we expected they would? I do not think the situation justifies any hon. member voting for the subamendment. The farmers of Canada are satisfied to comply with the regulations as at present applied, and under which, if they choose to ask for deferment of their service when called, they are sent back to till the soil, to work and fight as soldiers of production.
I should not like to conclude this first part of my remarks without a word of praise for the sons of the soil who volunteered for service, or who, when called under the present regulations, reported for service. What would Jean-Baptiste Montminy, from St. Just de Montmagny, think of such an amendment? Jean-Baptiste Montminy volunteered in the first days of the war and has seen service in Italy, and a month ago this man was awarded1 the Military Cross, with the following citation:
During the attack against hill 246 at Santa Maria he led his platoon to assault. After the machine-gunner was killed he took hold of the

The Address-Mr. Picard
machine-gun and ammunition and advanced in the direction of two nests of enemy machine-guns and by skilful manoeuvring of his arm succeeded in reducing them to silence.
Climbing the hill with his platoon, despite heavy enemy fire he operated on his own initiative an encircling move, and utilizing resourcefully geographic accidents he succeeded in dislodging the enemy who was then impeding the advance of the Canadian unit.
Here was a man who had tilled the soil. Here was a farmer from Quebec, who had enlisted and is keeping alive by his exploits the tradition of the old 22nd battalion of the last war.
As to those who are yet on the farm, they are by their labour and their energy serving on the home front to help feed the country, to help feed Britain and our allies.
One thing I should like to say just now. I am sure that French Canada will realize when this war is over that it owes more to men like Jean-Baptiste Montminy of St. Just, who was decorated in Italy; that it owes more to men like Flight Sergeant Marc Chabot, who was reported missing after an air raid in North Africa in 1941 and who since then has been presumed dead in action and whose father and grandparents are from St. Francois in my constituency; that it owes more to all its sons who have served in this war and who have vindicated its reputation, than it owes to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) and those who surround him and who share his views, or to the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix), who seconded this subamendment.
It might be opportune at this moment to see what the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency had to say in this debate, to examine his attitude during the past two years, and to form a conclusion as to the use it has been to his own province and to his own people. Speaking in this debate, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency criticized all Liberal administrations since 1900. He criticized the late Mr. Lapointe's statement in this house in September, 1939, as to Canada's participation, and called it a gesture of colonialism. If the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency was so much against what Mr. Lapointe said in 1939, why did he support him; why did he run in Montmorency as a straight Liberal in support of King and Lapointe in 1940? I remember a meeting in the good constituency of Quebec East, with which I have many links because for a long time I was secretary to the then hon. member for that constituency, Mr. Lapointe. Everyone wondered what would be said by the brave member for Quebec-Montmorency, who only a few months before had spoken against Canada's participation in the war. Everyone
wondered how he would act when the election came along. In Limoilou, in the large hall where most political campaigns in Quebec East are begun, we had our honourable colleague sitting in the front row. When his time came to speak he rose very pompously, bowed very nicely in the direction of the then Minister of Justice, Mr. Lapointe, and said, "My respected leader, Mr. Lapointe." Then he bowed a little more mildly in the direction of the then minister of pensions, now Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) and said, "My good friend, Mr. Power," and proceeded to support the Liberal party which was appealing to the people at that time.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that what the hon. member calls gestures of colonialism had been made before 1940, before that campaign opened. Why, then, did the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, who now criticizes every move made by the government, support the government at that time? I will tell you it was because he felt that the province of Quebec, and indeed the whole of Canada, were behind King and Lapointe. Why does he not cross the floor now and sit in the far corner? Again, because he has his nose in the wind; he wants to make sure whether the people of Quebec will follow King again in the next election, he senses that the people of my province, with those of the rest of Canada, at the next election will be behind Mackenzie King again, and he wants to play safe if he can. The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency tells everyone privately, "Well, I am just following the advice of Mr. Lapointe. I am staying within the party and trying to bring about reforms." That was what Mr. Lapointe said one day when he saw a few Liberals in Quebec form a group called L'Action Liberale Nationale; men who differed with the provincial government on no real question of principle but who did not agree with certain actions taken by that government. One of these men was a friend of Mr. Lapointe who, without trying to bring about any change within the party, had left to help form this other group. Mr. Lapointe said. "The Liberal party is broad enough to tolerate discussion within its ranks. Could they not have aired their views and differences within the party, instead of forming another party?" There is a great difference between that attitude and the one taken by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency in this house during the last few years. Mr. Lapointe meant that any reforms or alterations to be brought about in a party policy, or any differences of view, should be aired within the party councils rather than in public. Any member of the party whose views differ from those of the majority should endeavour in party caucus, by private conversations and in
The Address-Mr. Picard

group meetings to influence the views of the party and have the policy changed. Of course liberty of action should exist within any political organization. At one time or another any member of this house may vote against his party if his principles or ideals force him to do so. That may show the strength of mind of the individual member, and it also demonstrates the true democratic value of our parliamentary system. However, Mr. Lapointe's words, so often quoted by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, never meant that a man whose views differed radically and constantly with those of his party, on matters of national importance, should remain apparently within the party in order the better to stab it in the back.
When an hon. member differs with his party on a vital question, or with the views generally accepted by his friends, he should do as the hon. member for Gaspe did when he left the Conservative benches. We know he is still a Conservative, though of a different species-a different brand of the same make, only temporarily isolated from the flock for the duration of the war-yet he did the proper thing when he. stepped down into the realm of pseudo-independence. The same might be said of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion), who I understand has been called in to reply to my remarks. He entered this house not as a Conservative but as an independent, but it might be interesting to see what he was in the past. During the election of 1940, when the present Conservative party was called the National Government party, if that is the right thing to say-I want to be precise and correct

the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay was the chief organizer in Quebec for that party. We must believe, however, that later on he saw the light md became converted to a spirit of independence, so that he now sits in this house as an independent. He has done the right thing; he is against the government, and we know it, so he sits' in that corner. When the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond), the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix) and the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) felt that their views could not be reconciled with those of the Liberal party, they crossed the floor; they moved, shall I say, to another "block." I do not approve their views; but if they considered that their views and those of the Liberal party were irreconcilable, they did the right thing. I have more respect for those who, having views opposed to those of the government, cross the floor and fight from the opposition benches, than for those opportunists who try to get whatever prestige they may from being considered Liberals but who are always lurk-

ing in the dark, a dagger in hand, ready to stab in the back those with whom they still pretend at times to be associated.
While our late leader, Mr. Lapointe, was in this house the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, like many others who now invoke Lapointe's memory to try to justify certain attitudes, had not a word of friendship for him privately; yet in 1940 the hon. member rallied to the cause of the Liberal party and ran in Quebec-Montmorency as a Liberal. In his remarks a few days ago he criticized the policies of Laurier, which are a part of Canadian history. He criticized the stand taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the beginning of this war, which is a matter of record. He criticized the action taken in 1940, not many months before he ran as a Liberal; yet at the time he proclaimed himself as a Liberal and acknowledged King and Lapointe as his leaders.
Are these matters at issue in your part of the country?

The issues in all parts of the country are really the same; they mean the winning of the war. My hon. friend should realize that what I am doing now is trying to convince the house that the people of my own province are all really united against the isolationists, so that the hon. gentleman has no reason to interrupt what I am saying. I am trying to prove that in Quebec sentiment is as good as in any other part of the country, and that my compatriots should not be classed with some few members in this house, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency and others, who have taken the same attitude and spread the same doctrine at large in the province, believing that they can get more popularity by stating that they are against participation, and by criticizing every phase of the war effort. Let me tell them that they are mistaken. With the help of their near-seditious paper in Montreal, on the radio and on the platform they try to poison the minds of our population. And as we failed to counteract immediately, they may have influenced temporarily those of the less well informed elements and may have pleased a very small minority of people who accept their views. But the people of my province are intelligent enough that when we went and explained the situation in its true light they reacted with their usual good and sound judgment, and soon realized that their true friends were not those who tried to ring the bell of narrow provincialism, or to awaken racial prejudices, as some of them do in

The Address-Mr. Picard
Quebec, and as the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) never fails to do each time he rises to speak in the house.
In the early days of the war, soon after the declaration, it might have been possible that some who were not well informed in Quebec might have thought that some elements of the Anglo-Canadian population had been influenced more by their love for Great Britain than by Canada's interests, when they had pushed Canada into the war. I do not believe it was a fact. I was convinced we were going into the war because of our own interests. Ill-informed people might have been led to believe otherwise at that time. But after every country in Europe was involved, after the fall of France, after Pearl Harbor, was it still justifiable for any one in this country to be isolationist? I think everybody in my province, when the situation wras properly explained, understood that Canada was joining with all liberty-loving nations in preventing the enslaving of the world by the axis nations. Canada was acting to protect her sacred heritage of the past, and to ensure our liberty in the world of to-morrow.
I can assure the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, and all others who take the same attitude, that the people of Quebec, just as the people in the other provinces, have greater confidence than ever in the present administration. They are just as proud as other people throughout the country in the government's war record. They cannot overlook the fact that, due to wise administration by this government, Canada has accomplished a magnificent war effort, undreamed of by many, while at the same time disturbing as little as possible the life of the country.
They cannot overlook the fact so eloquently outlined yesterday by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), that Canadian farmers are more prosperous to-day than they were before the war, that industry has been mobilized, and that the working class is better off to-day than at any time before the war- and all that while Canada has mobilized vast armies, has enlarged its navy tenfold, and has equipped and trained the most magnificent air force and managed so efficiently the empire training scheme-and all that while Canada has helped so magnanimously to feed and equip Britain and the united nations.
And I say here that these extraordinary accomplishments have done more to make of Canada a great nation, an important sovereign
state, than can or will the wailing of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, and those who adopt the same attitude.
I am not more of an imperialist than the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency. I have just as much at heart the interests of Canada, and I want to point out to that hon. member that Canada evolved from colonial status to that of a great dominion, under Laurier, whose policies were criticized only a short time ago by 'the hon. member. Canada evolved under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) from the status of a dominion, as the word meant in 1911, to that of an autonomous nation within the empire, as meant by. the declaration of the imperial conference of 1926. Canada has continued to evolve from that condition to that of a sovereign state, again, under the present Prime Minister.
I attach more importance to the broad policies of the government than to the eradication of a few symbols of the past, to which the hon. member ties his policy, and that can and will be corrected by one simple gesture at the proper time.
