Mr. HOWARD C. GREEN (Vancouver South): Mr. Speaker, this evening I would ask hon. members for a few minutes to turn their thoughts to the west, not to the near west, the prairies, but far across Canada, over the Rocky Mountains, to the Pacific Coast, where they would find snowdrops and crocuses blooming -and', I must admit, might also find1 a little fog; and then to direct their thoughts farther out, across that vast ocean, the Pacific.
It is my purpose to-night to deal primarily with Canada's position in the war on the Pacific. Then I shall discuss the new Australian-New Zealand agreement signed less than three weeks ago. Following that, I shall touch upon British commonwealth defence and foreign policy.
But before doing so I wish to say a few words with respect to two points in the amendment to the address offered by my party, the Progressive Conservative party. Those two points are the failure of the government to provide adequately for the men and women in our forces and the protest contained in the amendment against the recent wages control order.
First, with respect to the men and women of the forces:	The young fighting men of
Canada have set a standard for the nation which has never been surpassed. I was very much pleased to read a statement by that great elder statesman Field-Marshal Smuts, where he said on December 8, referring to our present younger generation, that this war has proved that our generation is not degenerate, and accordingly that he looked forward with confidence and faith to the future.
Canada can expect great things from her young men and women on their return from this war. They will bring bold and forwardlooking leadership. They will bring a new and broader vision to this, their nation. In the meantime, however, what about those of us who are on the home front and, in particular, what about those of us who are members of the House of Commons of Canada? Our young men are going into heavier battles; there will be greater casualties as the year progresses. Canadians at home, particularly during this year, must never forget the personal aspect of waging war, that our fighting men are placing their lives between us and our enemies. They are making the greatest sacrifice possible; let there be no mistake about that. The very least we can do is to make certain that they and their dependents are cared for adequately, are treated in a spirit of gratitude rather than grudgingly. I regret to say that that is not being done by the government of Canada and I propose to give several examples.

My first reference is to the medical examination given to recruits. This has been far more thorough than was given to those of us .who enlisted in the last war and there has been far less chance for mistakes. Yet we find that only a small number of men who have been' taken on the strength as being in category "A" and then discharged as being in category "E" have been able to qualify for a pension. That is something I cannot understand. Last year I asked for a return, and the information received was that less than fifty per cent of the men who had enlisted in category "A" served overseas, come back and been discharged in category "E" .were able to get pensions. Of the men who served in Canada, only one in thirty-three could obtain a pension and yet, when they enlisted, they were placed in the top category and, when discharged, in the lowest.
The Pension Act is wrong, and it should be changed to provide that there shall be a definite presumption that a man's condition as recorded on his admission to service was in fact his condition and that any subsequent deterioration is due to service. It should be the responsibility of the government to overcome that presumption or else award the man a pension. Further, the insurance principle should be extended to men serving in Canada. It applied to them in the last war and it did in this war until some time in May, 1940. The present position is that a man must prove that his disability arose out of or was directly connected with service. A direct result of that provision in the law is, as I have mentioned, that only one in thirty-three of the men discharged in Canada under the conditions outlined has been able to qualify for a pension.
In another regard the government has not treated these men fairly. I refer to their pay and allowances on discharge. A man is given one month's pay and a clothing allowance which has recently been raised to $65. That is not sufficient to clothe a man coming out of the forces, and one month's pay is not sufficient to enable him to readjust himself and get settled in civilian life. I have had men come to my office who have served with our own Seaforth battalion which has given such gallant service in Sicily and Italy. They find that this allowance is not sufficient to purchase a proper outfit and it has proved a shock to their morale. They cannot understand why they should be treated in this way. This condition cannot be remedied too quickly.
As a third example, the government has failed to enact a Sparkman act for Canada. Members will recall that last year we had a debate lasting a whole afternoon on the advisability of setting up legislation of this kind

The Address-Mr. Green
in Canada. The Sparkman act is the United States act which protects the fighting man's home, protects him with regard to debt, mortgages, insurance, leases, loan interest and so on. Members of every party in the house spoke in favour of such an act, and so did the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). As reported at page 3055 of Hansard of May 26, 1943, he stated that a committee had been appointed to consider this legislation and had reported. He then went on to say:
I anticipate that action will be taken along lines which I feel ought to meet the situation.
And further on:
I can only assure the committee that every study will be made of the matter, and active consideration will be given to it.
Almost a year has gone by, but as far as I know no such provision has been made.
To sum up, I repeat that the government has failed to provide adequately for the men and women of the forces. The ministry seem to have little realization of the sacrifices that are being made, they go just far enough to save face and only that far after there has been a great deal of coaxing and prodding and long delay. So much for the men and women of the forces.
Then a word with regard to our protest against the recent wages control order, P.C. 9384. I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister (Mr.Mackenzie King) state to-day that there would probably be an amendment to that order in council. I think he would be well advised to go further and scrap the whole thing and start over again. When I read that order in council I was amazed at the government dealing in such a cavalier fashion with any group of law-abiding Canadian citizens, large or small. The whole tone of the order is punitive rather than friendly, and this at a time when labour generally has shown a keen desire to cooperate, has shown by and large a high sense of responsibility to Canada, as great a sense of responsibility as any other body of men or women in this country.
For example, the order in council provides for the setting up of a national board upon which the employees are to have only one representative out of six. This board must review the decisions or the directions of the regional boards which are on the spot and have a far greater knowledge of local conditions. The national board may of its own initiative, without a hearing of any kind, vary or revoke an order of a regional board. Then an iron-clad ceiling is clamped down on wage rates, and there are drastic terms outlawing strikes. The burden of proof is thrown on the accused, contrary to all our ideas of British justice. There is set up a dictatorship with regard to
prosecutions, which is placed in the hands of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). Finally, there is an intimation in the recital of the order in council that the order is necessary not only in war-goodness knows it is bad enough in war time-but also during the postwar period'. That period will be difficult enough even with friendliness and cooperation between all groups of Canadians, but with orders in council of this type there will be nothing but chaos. I urge that the order be cancelled and something at least approaching Canadianism substituted in its place.
I come now to Canada's position in the war on the Pacific. Our position in that theatre of war is most unsatisfactory. Although we are a nation on the Pacific and vitally interested in what goes on around the shores of that ocean, we are failing and have failed to accept our share of the responsibilities. Before Japan struck in December, 1941, we sent out our ill-fated and ill-equipped force to Hong Kong. I was saddened just last week to see a press dispatch covering the experience of a Chinese who had escaped from Hong Kong and returned to Canada. He reported the bayoneting of nine Canadian officers and men. He then went on to say that he had been in a prison camp with men of the Royal Rifles and the Winnipeg Grenadiers and that they had very little mechanical transport and were disappointed and angry over the delay in the arrival of their equipment. Some day, Mr. Speaker, there will be much more said about the failure to equip properly that force which was sent to Hong Kong. After Japan had struck; after great pressure from every sort of people in the Pacific province, and after, I believe, pressure from the United. States of America, the government finally established defence forces on the Pacific coast. Eventually some airmen were sent to Alaska, most of whom I believe have since gone to other parts, and then last summer a small task force was sent to Kiska with the United States forces which attacked that island. The Canadian troops did good work there; they made a good name for themselves and' upheld the reputation of Canadian fighting men. Now they have returned to Canada, and once again Australians, New Zealanders and the Americans are left to do the fighting in the Pacific war zone. If Canada continues in this way she will have very little voice in Pacific affairs, and she will deserve very little voice.
Why does the government adopt this policy in Pacific affairs? The answer is simple. It is because the troops on the coast, including the troops who went to Kiska, are home defence troops, and under the government's policy, not under the Canadian law, they cannot be
The Address-Mr. Green

sent to fight away from the American continent. That is the position despite the plebiscite vote, which was overwhelmingly yes. The result is, of course, that the government is in effect defying the expressed wish of the great majority of the Canadian people. These home defence troops on the Pacific coast cannot go abroad under the government's policy despite the fact that they are fully trained and equipped, and that those at least who went to Kiska are experienced, have a high morale and are eager to fight the Japanese. They are not so keen about going to Europe. I believe that questions have been asked throughout the force and there is a desire among them of their own free will to go and fight the Japanese. The government still maintains its policy despite the further fact that behind these Pacific coast troops there are in Canada thousands and thousands of other home defence troops piling up who can never be used in fighting unless that fighting takes place on Canadian soil. Finally, these troops are held in Canada despite the fact that Canada's duty is to do her full share in the war on the Pacific. And so I appeal to the Prime Minister of this country to stop this farce at once and send these troops to fight either beside the Australians and New Zealanders in the South Pacific or beside the Americans in the Central Pacific.
Canadians facing on the Pacific ocean are always greatly interested in what is done by our sister nations, Australia and New Zealand, because our outlook and our interests are much the same. We were therefore greatly interested in the agreement recently negotiated between Australia and New Zealand known as the Australian-New Zealand agreement, 1944. I think that agreement is of great importance not only to those of us who live on Canda's Pacific coast, but to all Canadians, in fact, to the whole British empire and to the different members of the united nations because it points the way to world peace. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that consideration should be given to printing this agreement and the accompanying press releases of the ministers of Australia and New Zealand in the Votes and Proceedings of this house so that the members may be able to give them more careful consideration. The agreement contains no secret clauses; everything is open and aboveboard. It begins with these words:
. . . having met in conference at Canberra from the 17th to the 21st of January, 1944, and desiring to maintain and strengthen the close and cordial relations between the two governments, do hereby enter into this agreement.
Then it goes on to define the objectives of Australian-New Zealand cooperation. It deals with such things as the prosecution of the

war, and with the armistice and the subsequent arrangements, and I would remind hon. members that the armistice period after this war is apt to be a long period, perhaps running into some years.
It also deals with the question of security and defence, and with civil aviation, outlining a new policy which Canadians should very carefully consider, a policy which among other things advocates international air trunk routes and the setting up of an international air transport authority.
Then it deals with dependencies and territories and with the welfare and advancement of the native peoples of the Pacific. It also provides for the calling of an international conference relating to the southwest and the south Pacific and for permanent machinery for collaboration and cooperation between Australia and New Zealand. That part of the agreement sets out measures whereby these two nations may cooperate for defence, and may collaborate in external policy; also for the development of commerce between them, for the full employment of Australians and New Zealanders, the highest standards of social security and the encouragement of missionary work and other activities directed toward the improvement of the welfare of native peoples. It goes on to invite other nations interested in the Pacific, of which Canada is one, to join Australia and New Zealand in promoting these objectives. That particular paragraph reads:
The two governments declare their desire to have the adherence to the objectives set out in the last preceding clause of any other government having or controlling territories in the Pacific.
I suggest that the government of Canada should give thought to collaborating with the Australians and New Zealanders under the terms of this agreement.
Then it provides for setting up a permanent secretariat with one branch in Australia and another in New Zealand. In explaining the agreement the minister of external affairs of Australia, Doctor Evatt, makes this statement which I think is of great importance to Canadians:
The war with its extension to the Pacific and its long sustained threat of utter disaster-
And these are words which Canadians would do well to mark, "its long sustained threat of utter disaster".
-has brought the two peoples closer together than ever before; it has made us realize that we can help each other only by pulling together in the struggles that still lie ahead; in winning, not only the war but the great struggle for improved standards in the years of post-war reconstruct on.

Doctor Evatt concluded with these words:
This agreement is in effect a permanent understanding between two nations which are completely autonomous and are at the same time united by a common allegiance to the King and also trustees for British interests and British civilization in the Pacific.
The prime minister of New Zealand, Mr. Fraser, used these words:
It is an agreement of positive value in the sense that it is directed against no other people; on the contrary, other powers are invited to adhere to the principles enunciated .... I should like to make it perfectly clear that neither the holding of this conference, nor the agreement resulting from it, is in any sense a departure from the principles of the British commonwealth of nations, membership of which is in the very forefront of the policy of both Australia and New Zealand.
The agreement therefore is a very practical step not only in the direction of security but also toward cooperation among all nations, in short, toward world peace. Obviously it would be absurd to say that it endangers world peace and equally absurd to say that any similar British commonwealth pact would do so; Doctor Evatt has suggested in his release that:
In the successful outcome of the present Australian-New Zealand consultations, there may well be a precedent of considerable value to other members of the British commonwealth.
That brings me to my final topic, namely, British commonwealth defence policy and foreign policy. Recently there has been considerable discussion concerning the advisability of working out a British commonwealth defence policy and foreign policy rather than each nation of the commonwealth having its own policy on these matters. It is a question which will require calm and careful consideration by the Canadian people, of whatever party. Personally, I believe that the condition of the world is such that a commonwealth policy on defence and on foreign affairs is advisable. Apparently the Canadian Prime Minister does not. He believes otherwise. He differs from such men of the empire as Field Marshal Smuts, Prime Minister of South Africa, and from the Prime Ministers of Australia and New Zealand, and Lord Halifax, a member of the British war cabinet; and he has rather summarily rejected the suggestions made by these men.
Now it can be agreed that all persons participating in this discussion have one common aim, namely, security and world peace. Prime Minister Smuts made that perfectly clear in his speech on the subject when he stressed as an objective human welfare, peace and security. Personally, therefore, I am hopeful that having
this one end in view, it will eventually be possible for all those who are involved to reach common ground.
Another fact upon which there is agreement is that all Canadians participating in this discussion are conscientiously thinking first of Canada's own interest. That must always be the basis for the foreign policy of Canada. What is the interest of our own nation? No one is questioning for a moment Canada's autonomy. That was settled long ago, not by a lot of politicans either, but by the men who fought in the last war, and it is being established further by young Canadians who are fighting in the present war.
So what about this question of a defence policy and a foreign policy? Before the war there was a very sketchy British commonwealth defence policy. There was no foreign policy; really, no part of the commonwealth had any foreign policy. Canada's foreign policy, as enunciated by the present government, was to have no commitments. We had no commitments to anyone; we buried our governmental head in the sand1 and let the rest of the world go by. That was one reason why the British peoples in the world were nearly wiped off the face of the earth in 1940 and 1941. During the war the reverse has been the case. The British commonwealth has had but one policy on defence, one foreign policy. We had to have such a policy; otherwise we would have perished, and with us civilization.
And so to-day, this very night, there are young Canadians fighting and dying beside young men from all other parts of the British commonwealth. We have in war time a commonwealth defence policy and a commonwealth foreign policy. What about after the war? Are we to continue in the same sensible way, or are we to have five or six defence policies and five or six foreign policies? Why not continue with the commonwealth policy and at the same time try to modernize and improve it?
Our Prime Minister says that Canada should aim at creating an effective international system. That is all very nice, all very general, and probably all very harmless. As reported at page 41 of the present debate he advocates creating an effective international system inside which the cooperation of all peace-loving countries is freely sought and given. No one can quarrel with that proposal, but it would not be affected or defeated by a commonwealth policy in addition. The Prime Minister thinks otherwise, because at page 42 he is reported to have said:
I maintain that apart from all questions as to how that common policy is to be reached, or enforced, such a conception runs counter to the establishment of effective world security.

Field-Marshal Smuts proposes in effect is a very practical step; it is that this trinity will have to maintain peace until an effective world organization can be set up, and that may take years.

The record of the governments led by the present Prime Minister of Canada in international affairs is not as good as it might be. He points out in this book that in 1924 Great Britain and France brought in a protocol the effect of which would have been to put teeth into the League of Nations, to give the league some force to back up its decisions. The debate was finished when the vote was taken.

I should like to quote from page 1063 of Hansard of February 19, 1937. At that time I had placed on Hansard a table from the dominion bureau of statistics giving the exports of nickel from 1929 to 1936, after which I made this statement:
Against whom are we arming? What potential aggressor is more aggressive to-day? Oh, I know that bogeymen have been trotted out in this chamber. It has been suggested that it might be Italy, it might be Germany, it might be Japan.
That is where the Minister of Mines and Resources stopped, but Hansard does not stop there. It goes on:
I cannot suppose that the government has any real fear of the intentions of the'e nations, for I noticed in the figures I have just read that Canada is shipping nickel to them. Knowing that we control the major part of the world's nickel supplies, I cannot believe that we would ship to them material which we feared would be returned to us in the form of high explosives. Surely those who talked about the Italians bombing this House of Commons did not imagine that the government of the day would allow us to send them the nickel with which they made those bombs, or did they?
That is the rest of the paragraph which the Minister of Mines and Resources so conveniently omitted to quote.

I should like to quote from the same speech of the hon. member. On page 1059 of Hansard of February 19, 1937, a few pages prior to that from which he quoted, I find the following:
I speak for my colleagues and myself when I say most categorically that we are opposed to the increases in the defence estimates.
Then in the same quotation which my hon. friend just gave there is a first part which he left out. This reads:
May I now state the three reasons why I cannot vote for the increase in armaments. First, I do not feel that the government has shown that we are in any way more menaced this year than we were last year. This group has not said that it is not in favour of defence, but we are opposed to an increase in the defence estimates because it has not yet been demonstrated that the danger has become any greater now than it was twelve months or twenty-four months ago.
Then he continues with what he said in regard to nickel. He knows quite well that Canada could not have stopped exporting nickel unless she stopped the export of that commodity to every country in the world.

362	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Ross (Moose Jaw)
Not at all.

Further on in the same speech as reported on page 1064 of Hansard, there is a full sentence, as follows:
I object to increased armaments.
No matter how much the hon. member wants to read Hansard, if he goes back to the debates of 1937, 1938 and 1939 he will find that his party was against increasing any estimates for defence when we were badly in need of them.

I was paired with the hon. member for Merrier (Mr. Jean). Had I voted, I would have voted for the amendment.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I was paired with the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). Had I voted, I would have voted against the amendment.
I was paired with the hon. member for Mereier (Mr. Jean). Had I voted I would have voted against the motion.
Is there not a rule, Mr. Speaker, that any hon. member in the house at the time of a division must vote?
I should prefer not to give an opinion on that point at the moment.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is a rule of the house

that immediately the address has been agreed to the house then appoints the two committees of the whole house, the committee of supply and the committee of ways and means. I therefore move:
That this house will, on Friday next, resolve itself into a committee to consider of a supply to be granted to His Majesty.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE

speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Prime Minister) moved:
That on Friday next this house resolve itself into a committee to consider of the ways and means for raising the supply to be granted to His Majesty.
Motion agreed to.
It being twenty-five minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday February 11, 1944
